META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 4.1 (9 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Frequency distribution tables (ungrouped and grouped data)
• Measures of central tendency: mean, mode and median (ungrouped and grouped data)
• Representation of data: histograms, frequency polygons and ogives
• Interpretation of data from tables and graphs
• Importance of collecting, organizing and interpreting data in making effective decisions
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) organise data using frequency distribution tables
b) calculate the mean, mode and median of ungrouped and grouped data
c) represent data using appropriate statistical graphs
d) interpret data presented in tables and graphs
e) appreciate the importance of collecting, organising and interpreting data in making effective decisions
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical thinking and problem solving: learners compare two sets of marks, analyse the evidence and justify predictions about the next steps for learners and teachers.
• Communication and collaboration: learners discuss and defend their interpretations of the data in groups and present findings to the class.
• Digital literacy: learners may use calculators or spreadsheets to organise and graph data.
• Learning to learn: learners revise their statistical model of the data as new measures and representations are introduced.
UNIT.values:
• Integrity: learners record and report data honestly without altering scores.
• Responsibility: learners use data to make fair and informed decisions about learning.
• Unity: learners work cooperatively in groups to analyse and interpret data.
UNIT.sep:
• Analyzing and interpreting data: learners order scores, build frequency tables, compute averages and interpret graphs.
• Developing and using models: learners build and revise a statistical model (table, measures, graph) of the two subjects' performance.
• Using mathematics and computational thinking: learners calculate mean, median and mode and use them to compare data sets.
• Engaging in argument from evidence: learners justify predictions about next steps using statistical evidence.
• Asking questions and defining problems: learners add questions to the Driving Question Board.
UNIT.pcis:
• Education for sustainable development / decision making: learners use data to make evidence-based decisions.
• Life skills (critical thinking, decision making): learners interpret results to choose appropriate actions.
• Citizenship: learners understand how data supports fair planning in school and community.
UNIT.careers:
• Statistician: collects and analyses data to inform decisions, for example at the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics.
• Teacher: uses class results to plan remedial teaching.
• Data analyst: summarises and visualises data for organisations in Nairobi.
• Agricultural extension officer: analyses crop yield data from farms in the Rift Valley.
• Economist or business manager: uses data to plan and forecast.
UNIT.focus: This unit is anchored in a comparison of 20 learners' scores in two subjects, where one set is high and the other is low. Learners organise, summarise, represent and interpret the data, building a statistical model across the lessons. They use it to predict what learners and teachers should do next.
UNIT.phenomenon: Learners are given the test scores of the same 20 students in two subjects. Subject 1: 72, 85, 90, 67, 78, 81, 95, 88, 74, 69, 82, 76, 91, 84, 77, 70, 89, 73, 80, 86. Subject 2: 35, 42, 27, 58, 44, 31, 60, 29, 15, 30, 32, 51, 60, 11, 13, 32, 23, 18, 21, 45. They arrange each set of scores in ascending order and discuss whether the learners passed or failed. They compare the two subjects and use their findings to predict the next steps for the learners and the two subject teachers. It is puzzling because the same students scored very high in one subject and very low in the other. The raw lists make it hard to see patterns, spread or what action is needed without organising and summarising the data.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Two Kenyan football teams in the Kisumu league with the same number of goals but different consistency across matches.
• A farmer in Kericho recording daily tea leaf yields and needing a typical value to plan.
• A school canteen in Nairobi recording daily sales of mandazi to decide how many to prepare.
• Daily maximum temperatures in Mombasa and Nakuru compared to decide what to expect.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables?
2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Phenomenon – learners predict, order the two sets of scores in ascending order, discuss pass or fail, and raise questions for the DQB.
Lesson 2: Frequency distribution tables for ungrouped data – tally and organise the scores.
Lesson 3: Grouped frequency distribution tables – choose class intervals and classify the scores of both subjects.
Lesson 4: Mean, mode and median of ungrouped data – compare the two subjects.
Lesson 5: Mean, mode and median of grouped data – estimate the measures from the grouped tables.
Lesson 6: Representation of data I – histograms and frequency polygons of the two subjects.
Lesson 7: Representation of data II – cumulative frequency and ogives; estimate the median and quartiles.
Lesson 8: Interpretation of data – read tables and graphs to compare the subjects and predict next steps for learners and teachers.
Lesson 9: Importance of collecting, organising and interpreting data in making effective decisions – final model revision and recommendations answering the driving question.

LESSONS.title: The Two Sets of Scores: Phenomenon Launch
LESSONS.aresKeywords: raw data, ascending order, score, highest, lowest, range, pass mark, pass, fail, pattern, spread, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon: the same 20 learners in a Kisumu day secondary school scored very high in Subject 1 and very low in Subject 2. Learners predict, arrange both lists in ascending order, decide who passed or failed, and raise questions showing that raw lists are hard to read without organising and summarising data.
slo.knowledge: Raw data can be arranged in ascending order to see the highest score, lowest score and pass/fail at a glance. With a pass mark of 50 out of 100, all 20 learners pass Subject 1 (lowest 67, highest 95, range 28) while only 4 pass Subject 2 (51, 58, 60, 60) and 16 fail (lowest 11, highest 60, range 49). The raw lists still raise questions about patterns, spread and what action is needed.
slo.skills: Arranging data in ascending order; reading the highest, lowest and range from ordered data; counting passes and fails against a pass mark; making and justifying predictions from evidence; asking investigable questions (NGSS practice: Asking Questions and Defining Problems; Analyzing and Interpreting Data).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about what data can reveal; honesty and accuracy when recording scores; respect for learners and teachers by treating reasons for scores as hypotheses and not blame; cooperation in groups of 4.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? 2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the launch lesson. It creates the need to know: the raw lists hide patterns, spread and the action needed. The questions on the Driving Question Board (DQB) drive Lessons 2 to 9, where learners will build frequency tables, calculate measures, draw graphs and finally write recommendations for Madam Achieng.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Seat groups so that no learner's marks are singled out publicly; the scores are labelled Learner 1 to Learner 20 only. Remind learners that the scores describe test results, not a person's worth, and that we do not blame any teacher or learner.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng, the Deputy Principal of a day secondary school in Kisumu near Lake Victoria, gives the Grade 10 class the test scores of the same 20 learners in two subjects, and asks them to use the data to decide next steps. Subject 1 is taught by Mr. Otieno and Subject 2 by Mrs. Wanjiku. Learners first predict what they expect, then work in groups of 4 to arrange both lists in ascending order, identify highest and lowest scores, and use the class pass mark of 50 to count passes and fails (20 pass Subject 1; 4 pass and 16 fail Subject 2). They notice the puzzle: the same learners did very well in one subject and poorly in the other. Because the ordered lists still do not show patterns or spread clearly, learners raise questions and open the Driving Question Board with the driving question: How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps? They build an initial model of what they think is happening and what they need to find out.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in groups of 4. They are told: 'Madam Achieng, the Deputy Principal, has the test scores of the same 20 Grade 10 learners in Subject 1 and Subject 2. Mr. Otieno teaches Subject 1 and Mrs. Wanjiku teaches Subject 2.' Before seeing any numbers, each learner writes in their notebook: (a) Do you expect the 20 learners to do equally well in both subjects? (b) What would you look for in the scores to decide who passed? (c) What do you think Madam Achieng will do next? They share predictions in their group and record one group prediction on manila paper. Then they are shown the two raw lists (in the order of Learner 1 to Learner 20): Subject 1: 72, 85, 90, 67, 78, 81, 95, 88, 74, 69, 82, 76, 91, 84, 77, 70, 89, 73, 80, 86. Subject 2: 35, 42, 27, 58, 44, 31, 60, 29, 15, 30, 32, 51, 60, 11, 13, 32, 23, 18, 21, 45. They look quickly at the lists and revise or confirm their prediction, writing one sentence on what they notice.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Imagine you are Madam Achieng in the staffroom in Kisumu with two lists of marks. Before you touch a pen, what do you expect?' Give each learner 2 minutes of silent writing. Then say: 'Turn to your group and share. Everyone must speak.' Circulate and listen for predictions such as 'same learners so same marks'. Display the raw lists and say: 'Look for 30 seconds without writing. What do you notice first?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking, then cold-call 4 learners from different groups. Ask: 'Which list looks higher? How can you tell?' and 'Does the order of the numbers help you?' Record the learners' words on the board under the heading 'What we notice' without correcting them. Ask one learner: 'Learner 7 scored 95 in Subject 1 and 60 in Subject 2. What does that tell us, and what does it not tell us?' Do not give reasons for the difference.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction first): committing to a written prediction before seeing the data exposes learners' prior ideas (for example that a learner who is strong in one subject is strong in all) so that the later evidence can confirm or challenge them. Think-Pair-Share builds confidence before whole-class talk.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every learner has a written prediction with a reason in their notebook before the data are shown; (2) at least 4 of 5 groups record a group prediction on manila paper; (3) learners can state at least one observation that compares the lists, such as 'Subject 1 numbers look bigger'; (4) learners avoid blaming statements and use words like 'may' or 'could'. Note learners who assume the same learners must score the same in both subjects, for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives a printed copy (or a copy written on the board) of both raw lists. Step 1: Each learner in the group arranges ONE list in ascending order (two learners per subject) and the pairs then swap and check each other's work. The correct ordered lists are: Subject 1: 67, 69, 70, 72, 73, 74, 76, 77, 78, 80, 81, 82, 84, 85, 86, 88, 89, 90, 91, 95. Subject 2: 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 23, 27, 29, 30, 31, 32, 32, 35, 42, 44, 45, 51, 58, 60, 60. They check that each list still has 20 scores (n = 20). Step 2: They record the lowest score, highest score and range (highest minus lowest) for each subject: Subject 1 lowest 67, highest 95, range 28; Subject 2 lowest 11, highest 60, range 49. Step 3: Using the class pass mark of 50 out of 100, they draw a line on each ordered list and count passes and fails: Subject 1, 20 pass and 0 fail; Subject 2, 4 pass (51, 58, 60, 60) and 16 fail. They note on manila paper that 7 learners in Subject 2 scored 40 or more, and record the table 'Subject | Lowest | Highest | Range | Pass | Fail'. Step 4: Groups write what they notice about the two subjects and what they still cannot tell from the lists.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Each pair takes one list. Cross out each score on the raw list as you copy it so that none is missed or repeated.' Circulate; ask 'How do you know you have all 20 scores?' Prompt a check: 'Count your ordered list. Is it 20?' Watch for common errors such as omitting a repeated 32 or 60 in Subject 2, or ordering 9 after 10. For groups that finish early ask: 'If the pass mark was 40, how many would pass Subject 2?' (7). Pause the class and say: 'Hands down. In your group, find the lowest in Subject 1 and the highest in Subject 2. What do you notice?' (67 is higher than 60.) WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups to report the range for each subject and 2 groups to report passes and fails. Say: 'Let us record our results in one class table on the board.' Ask: 'Can you tell from these ordered lists whether most scores are near the middle, or spread out evenly?' Let learners struggle and say this is difficult. Do not compute the mean or median yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data organisation with a claim-evidence check: ordering the scores converts an unreadable list into one where highest, lowest and pass/fail are visible at a glance, and learners use the line at 50 as evidence for their claims. Cross-checking with a partner builds accuracy and a habit of verifying data (NGSS: Analyzing and Interpreting Data).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) both ordered lists are correct and contain 20 scores, including two 32s and two 60s in Subject 2; (2) learners correctly state lowest, highest and range (67, 95, 28; 11, 60, 49); (3) learners state 20 pass in Subject 1 and 4 pass and 16 fail in Subject 2 using the pass mark of 50; (4) learners can say what the ordered lists still do not show (for example how scores cluster or spread). Use a quick tally of groups with correct counts; reteach ordering with a smaller sample (for example 5 scores) for any group that gets it wrong.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners hold a whole-class discussion using the evidence from their tables. They answer in their groups: (1) Did the learners pass or fail Subject 1? Subject 2? Use the numbers. (2) Can we say the 20 learners are 'good' or 'weak'? Why or why not? (3) What do you think Madam Achieng should do for Mr. Otieno's class and for Mrs. Wanjiku's class? (4) What might explain the difference? Each group writes at least two possible reasons as hypotheses (for example 'the test may have been harder', 'the topics may not have been revised', 'the teaching method could differ') and one piece of data we would need to test each. They then complete a sentence frame: 'The evidence shows that ___, but we cannot yet say ___ because ___.' Groups present to the class from their manila paper.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use your numbers: who passed, and how do you know?' Then: 'The same 20 learners scored between 67 and 95 in Subject 1 and between 11 and 60 in Subject 2. Can we say these learners are weak? Turn and talk for 1 minute.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Press for evidence: 'Which number supports your claim?' When a learner offers a cause as a fact (for example 'Mrs. Wanjiku is not teaching well'), respond: 'That is a hypothesis, not yet a fact. What data would we need to test it?' Write 'Hypothesis' and 'Fact from the data' in two columns on the board and sort the learners' statements with the class. Facts: all 20 pass Subject 1; 16 fail Subject 2. Hypotheses: harder test, less revision, teaching method. Ask: 'What decisions could Madam Achieng make today, and what decisions would be unfair without more data?' Invite 2 groups to present their sentence frames. Use local analogies if needed: 'If one farmer in the Rift Valley gets a poor maize yield from one plot, do we blame the farmer or check the soil, rain and seed first?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a Fact vs Hypothesis sort: learners separate what the data show from what is only suggested, building scientific habits of mind and fairness. The sentence frame forces them to state the limits of the evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners use specific numbers (20 pass; 4 pass, 16 fail; lowest 67 and 11) to support claims; (2) at least 3 groups place causes under 'Hypothesis' and not 'Fact'; (3) learners recognise that the difference is between subjects, not that all learners are weak; (4) each group can name data needed to test one hypothesis (for example a second test or topic-by-topic marks). Listen for blame language and redirect it to evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners read the driving question aloud: 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' Each learner writes 2 questions on sticky notes or paper strips about what they want to find out, thinking about patterns, spread, typical scores and actions needed. Groups sort their notes into categories such as 'How to organise the data', 'How to find a typical score', 'How to compare spread', 'How to show it in graphs' and 'What decisions to make'. Each group posts its 3 best questions on the DQB. Possible learner questions: 'How many learners got each score?', 'What is the average score in each subject?', 'Is there a faster way to see where most scores lie?', 'How can we show the two subjects in a picture?', 'Which learners need help?', 'What more data do we need?' The class then links the board to the two KICD inquiry questions: How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'The ordered lists helped us, but they did not tell us everything. What are you still wondering? Write 2 questions: one about how to organise or summarise the scores, and one about what action to take.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Circulate and push for investigable questions: 'Can we answer that using the data? What would we calculate or draw?' Convert yes/no questions: 'Is Subject 2 hard?' becomes 'How can we compare the spread of scores in Subject 2 with Subject 1?' Ask each group to post 3 questions and cold-call 5 groups to read one aloud and say where it fits. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before asking the class: 'Which questions look similar? Which can we answer first?' Group them with the class into 4-5 themes and label each with a lesson cluster (frequency tables, measures of the typical score, graphs, comparing, decisions) without giving answers. Add the two KICD key inquiry questions to the board on strips. Say: 'We will return to this board at the end of each lesson to move questions to answered.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question sorting: learner-generated questions give ownership of the unit, make the need for frequency tables, measures and graphs visible, and allow the class to track growing understanding across Lessons 2 to 9.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) every learner contributes at least 2 questions; (2) at least half of the posted questions can be answered with data (for example about frequency, average, spread, graphs); (3) groups can sort questions into themes; (4) at least one question asks what more data is needed. Keep the notes to identify misconceptions, such as using only the highest score to judge a class.

framework.learnerExperience: On manila paper, each group draws an initial model titled 'What we think is happening, and what we need to find out'. The model includes: (1) a simple box showing the two ordered lists with lowest, highest, range and pass/fail counts; (2) arrows linking 'Subject 1: all 20 pass, scores 67 to 95' and 'Subject 2: 4 pass, 16 fail, scores 11 to 60' to Madam Achieng's decisions; (3) a section 'Possible reasons (hypotheses)' with 'may' or 'could' wording; (4) a section 'Tools we think we need' (for example tables, a typical score, pictures or graphs); (5) a section 'Next steps we predict' for the learners, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku. Groups do a gallery walk, adding one question or suggestion on a sticky note to another group's model. Finally each learner completes an exit ticket: 'One thing the ordered lists showed me is ___. One thing they did not show me is ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw your first model. It will be revised many times, so it is fine if it is incomplete. Include what the data show, what you guess, and what you need.' Circulate with prompts: 'Where did you use the pass mark?', 'Which parts of your model are facts and which are hypotheses?', 'What would you add if you could do one more calculation?' Set the gallery walk for 6 minutes and ask each learner to leave one question or suggestion on another group's model. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What do the models have in common?' Cold-call 3 learners. Say: 'Keep your model; in Lesson 2 we start organising the scores with tally marks and frequency tables.' Collect exit tickets. Photograph or keep the models for revision in later lessons. Close with Madam Achieng's request: 'Use the data to decide next steps. We are not ready to decide yet. What do we need?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial model building with gallery walk feedback: externalising ideas in a diagram makes thinking visible, separates evidence from guesses, and creates a baseline model that learners will revise in each later lesson as they gain new tools (Developing and Using Models).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) models include correct pass/fail counts (20 pass; 4 pass, 16 fail) and the correct lowest, highest and range; (2) hypotheses are labelled as possible and not as facts; (3) models name at least one tool or data still needed; (4) exit tickets show that learners can say what ordering revealed (highest, lowest, pass/fail) and what it did not (patterns, spread, typical score, action). Learners whose exit ticket shows no limit of ordered data get extra support in Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Did every learner correctly order both lists, including the repeated 32 and 60 in Subject 2? Which groups used the pass mark of 50 accurately? Did learners treat causes as hypotheses or did blame statements about Mr. Otieno, Mrs. Wanjiku or the learners occur, and how did I redirect them? Which DQB questions will be answered in Lessons 2 to 9, and which need extra data collection? What prior ideas about marks, averages or pass/fail did I notice that need to be revisited?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the same 20 learners scored between 67 and 95 in Subject 1 (range 28, all 20 pass) and between 11 and 60 in Subject 2 (range 49, only 4 pass and 16 fail at a pass mark of 50). Ordering the scores made the highest, lowest and pass/fail easy to see.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that arranging raw data in ascending order shows the highest, lowest and pass/fail at a glance, but it does not clearly show patterns, spread or the typical score. Reasons for the difference are only hypotheses until we have more data.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The difference is between the subjects, so we cannot say all 20 learners are weak. To decide next steps for the learners, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku, we need to organise and summarise the data with tables, typical values and graphs, which is what we will do in the coming lessons.

LESSONS.title: Frequency Distribution Tables for Ungrouped Data: Tallying the Two Sets of Scores
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; extend to 80 minutes if a double lesson is available)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: frequency distribution table, tally marks, frequency, ungrouped data, score, total frequency, n = 20, pass mark 50, Subject 1, Subject 2

slo.purpose: Learners build ungrouped frequency distribution tables (score, tally, frequency) for the two sets of 20 scores using tally marks grouped in fives, and check that the frequencies add up to n = 20. They then judge how much the tables help to answer the driving question and what the tables still cannot show.
slo.knowledge: A frequency distribution table lists each score with a tally and the number of times it occurs (its frequency, f). The frequencies must add up to the total number of scores, n = 20. In Subject 1 every one of the 20 scores occurs exactly once (f = 1 for each). In Subject 2, 32 and 60 each occur twice and the other 16 scores occur once, which gives 18 different scores and a total of 20.
slo.skills: Organising data using tally marks grouped in fives; constructing an ungrouped frequency table from the ordered lists; checking totals (sum of f = n); identifying the most frequent scores; analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP 4); using mathematics and computational thinking (NGSS SEP 5) to check that the frequencies add to 20; constructing explanations from evidence (NGSS SEP 6).
slo.attitudes: Accuracy and patience when tallying; honesty in checking and correcting counts; cooperation in groups of 4; curiosity about what the data can and cannot tell us; willingness to say 'we need more data' instead of guessing reasons.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? 2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1, learners put both raw lists in ascending order and saw the highest, lowest and pass/fail counts, but found the raw lists still raise questions about patterns, spread and action needed. Lesson 2 gives learners their first organising tool, the ungrouped frequency table. The tables show that Subject 1 has every score appearing once and Subject 2 has two repeated scores (32 and 60). This creates the need for grouping in Lesson 3 (not taught here) and the need for summary measures in Lesson 4.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Use a pencil and ruler on manila paper or exercise books. Learners should remain seated while tallying to avoid accidents with sharp markers or tape. Be sensitive about the scores: refer to Learner 1 to Learner 20 by number, do not shame learners for low scores, and treat the Subject 2 scores as data about the subject, not as a judgement of the learners.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng, the Head of Department at a day secondary school in Kisumu, still has the same 20 Grade 10 learners' scores in Subject 1 (Mr. Otieno's class) and Subject 2 (Mrs. Wanjiku's class). Last lesson the class ordered the scores and saw that all 20 learners passed Subject 1 (lowest 67) while only 4 of 20 passed Subject 2 (lowest 11), using the pass mark of 50. The ordered lists are still long, so Madam Achieng asks: 'Can we organise the scores so that a busy teacher can see how often each score occurs?' Learners first predict what a table of the scores might look like and how many times each score will appear. They then build ungrouped frequency tables with tally marks grouped in fives, one table for each subject, and check that the frequencies add up to 20. In the Explain Phase they compare the two tables. Subject 1 has 20 different scores, each with f = 1, so the table is as long as the list and shows little. Subject 2 has 18 different scores with 32 and 60 each occurring twice. Learners discuss what the tables help them see and what questions remain about spread and action needed, and they treat reasons for the difference as hypotheses, not facts. They add new questions to the Driving Question Board and add the frequency table to the class model of how data helps predict next steps for the learners and teachers.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall Lesson 1: both ordered lists and the pass/fail counts (20 pass in Subject 1; 4 pass and 16 fail in Subject 2). Each learner receives the ascending lists. Subject 1: 67, 69, 70, 72, 73, 74, 76, 77, 78, 80, 81, 82, 84, 85, 86, 88, 89, 90, 91, 95. Subject 2: 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 23, 27, 29, 30, 31, 32, 32, 35, 42, 44, 45, 51, 58, 60, 60. Learners individually write answers to: (a) 'If we make a table showing each score and how many learners got it, how many rows might Subject 1 have? Subject 2?' (b) 'Will any score appear more than once? Which subject is more likely to have repeats?' (c) 'Will a table help Madam Achieng decide the next steps?' They share predictions with a partner, then record them on a 'Predictions' column on the board and in their books.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Driving Question: 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' Say: 'Yesterday we ordered the scores. Madam Achieng says the lists are still long. How can we show how often each score occurs?' Give 2 minutes of silent individual writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question before taking responses. Cold-call 4 learners for predicted row counts and 3 learners for predictions about repeats; ask each 'What in the ordered list makes you say that?' Do not confirm or correct yet. Record all predictions on the board under 'Predictions' with the learner's reasoning. Say: 'Hold on to these. We will test them with our own tally tables.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with Think-Pair-Share: committing to a written prediction before tallying creates a cognitive conflict or confirmation that makes learners care about the result. Pair sharing lets learners hear other reasoning before they test their own ideas against the evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (1) write a numerical prediction for the number of rows, (2) give a reason that refers to the ordered list (for example 'the Subject 2 list has 32 twice and 60 twice'), and (3) distinguish repeats from no repeats. Note learners who predict that Subject 1 will have the same number of rows as scores (an accurate prediction) and those who do not look at the lists. Tally common predictions on the board to plan the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners build the ungrouped frequency distribution tables. Step 1: Teacher models the tally process using a few scores from Subject 2 (for example the score 32: strike the first tally, then the second), showing that the fifth tally crosses the first four so tallies are grouped in fives. Step 2: Each group draws two tables on manila paper with three columns: Score (x), Tally, Frequency (f). Step 3: Using the ORIGINAL RAW lists as in the order given (Subject 1: 72, 85, 90, 67, 78, 81, 95, 88, 74, 69, 82, 76, 91, 84, 77, 70, 89, 73, 80, 86; Subject 2: 35, 42, 27, 58, 44, 31, 60, 29, 15, 30, 32, 51, 60, 11, 13, 32, 23, 18, 21, 45), one learner reads out the scores one by one, a second tallies in the table, a third crosses off each score in the raw list, and the fourth checks. The group then swaps roles for the second subject. Step 4: For each table, groups write the frequency as a number next to the tally and add the frequency column. They must get 20 for each table. Step 5: Groups record how many different scores each subject has (20 in Subject 1; 18 in Subject 2) and which scores have a frequency greater than 1 (none in Subject 1; 32 and 60 in Subject 2). Groups that finish early identify which row of the Subject 2 table includes Learner 7's score (60, which has f = 2) and which score in Subject 1 belongs to Learner 7 (95, f = 1).
framework.teacherMoves: Model for 3 minutes on the board, then circulate. Say: 'Read each score aloud, make one tally, and cross it off the raw list so nothing is counted twice.' Ask groups: 'Where did you put the fifth tally?' and 'How do you know you have not missed a score?' Intervene with questions, not answers, if a group's total is not 20: 'Your frequencies add to 19. Where might a score be missing? How can you find it?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before offering a hint. Tell groups to compare with the ordered list from Lesson 1 to check for repeats. Cold-call 3 groups to report total frequency for Subject 1 and 3 groups for Subject 2 and record on the board. Expected: Subject 1 total 20, all f = 1; Subject 2 total 20, with 32 and 60 each f = 2. Do not tell learners why scores differ between subjects; if asked, say 'Good question. The table cannot tell us why. We will write that as a question for the Driving Question Board.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with role rotation (reader, tallier, checker, recorder) and self-checking against the known total n = 20. Learners build understanding that a table is a systematic count: each score is counted once, and a check total shows whether the count is accurate (using mathematics and computational thinking, NGSS SEP 5).
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) tallies grouped in fives with the fifth tally crossing the first four; (2) a row for every score with tally and frequency in the correct column; (3) frequency columns adding to 20 in both tables; (4) correct identification that Subject 1 has no repeats and Subject 2 repeats 32 and 60; (5) groups that find and correct their own counting errors. Note groups that count tally marks wrongly (for example counting a group of five as 4) and address this in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their finished tables to answer questions in a whole-class discussion and then in a short written response. Discussion questions: (1) 'Did your predictions match your tables? Which prediction was correct and which changed?' (2) 'Subject 1 has 20 different scores, each with f = 1. What does this table show that the ordered list did not? What does it not show?' (3) 'Subject 2 has 32 and 60 each with f = 2. How does the table show this?' (4) 'Why must the frequencies add up to 20? What does it mean if they add to 19 or 21?' (5) 'Madam Achieng wants to see quickly where most learners scored. Can she do that from the Subject 1 table? From the Subject 2 table?' Learners should explain that the ungrouped tables are accurate and show the repeats, but they are long and, for Subject 1, are almost as long as the list; the tables do not yet show clusters or spread clearly, so another way of organising is needed (to be developed in Lesson 3). Learners then complete a claim-evidence-reasoning statement: 'Claim: ___. Evidence from the table: ___. Reasoning: ___.' For example: 'Claim: the ungrouped table for Subject 1 does not make the pattern clearer. Evidence: all 20 scores have f = 1 and the table has 20 rows. Reasoning: a table that is as long as the list does not summarise the data.' Learners also write one honest statement about causes, such as 'The table cannot tell us why Subject 2 scores are lower; reasons like the test difficulty, teaching method or revision time could be possible, but we need more data.'
framework.teacherMoves: Ask the questions one at a time with WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before each response. Use a Talk Move: 'Who can add on to what Learner 5 said?' Cold-call 5 learners in total across the questions, including at least 2 who did not speak in the Observe Phase. Press for evidence: 'Point to the row in your table that shows that.' When a learner says 'Subject 1 is easy and Subject 2 is hard', respond: 'That could be one explanation. Is it in our data? What data would we need to test it?' and write the hypothesis on a 'Hypotheses to test' chart. Revisit the Predict Phase predictions on the board: tick those supported by evidence and amend others with the learners' words. Emphasise: 'The total frequency is 20 because there are 20 learners. A table that does not add to 20 has a counting error.' Close by saying: 'Our tables are accurate, but they are still long. What would help Madam Achieng see where most scores lie? Keep that question for the next lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a whole-class Talk Move discussion (NGSS SEP 6, constructing explanations): learners must link their statements to specific rows in their tables. Treating reasons for the difference as hypotheses to test teaches the difference between what data show and what we infer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that written CER statements: (1) cite specific frequencies (for example 'f = 2 for 32 and 60'); (2) correctly state that sum of f = 20 for both tables; (3) acknowledge a limitation of the ungrouped table (long, no clear clusters for Subject 1); (4) use cautious language ('may', 'could', 'we need more data') for causes. Look for misconceptions: thinking that frequency means the score itself, or that the table shows who scored what (it does not identify individual learners). Collect 5 written responses as an exit check.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the question 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' Individually, each learner writes one thing the frequency tables helped them see (for example 'Subject 2 has two repeated scores, 32 and 60') and one new question on a sticky note or paper strip (for example 'How can we show where most Subject 2 scores lie without so many rows?', 'Why do Subject 2 scores spread from 11 to 60?', 'What is the typical score in each subject?', 'How do we make the Subject 1 table shorter?'). They post notes on the DQB under headings: 'What the tables showed', 'Questions we can answer next' and 'Questions that need more data' (for example 'Why did learners score differently in the two subjects?'). The class sorts the questions together and links two or three to future lessons (grouping, averages, graphs).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our DQB should show what we know and what we still need. Write what the tables helped you see and one new question.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before sharing. Cold-call 4 learners to read and post a question and ask the class 'Which heading does this belong under, and why?' Highlight questions that cannot be answered from our data (causes) and place them under 'Questions that need more data'. Group similar questions and point out those the class will return to: 'The question about showing where most scores lie is exactly what we will tackle when we group scores into classes.' Do not promise answers to questions that require extra data collection, but say 'We will decide what data we would need to collect.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question sorting: making learners' questions visible and classifying them as answerable now, answerable later in the unit, or needing more data builds ownership of the inquiry and teaches that statistical questions depend on the data available (NGSS SEP 1, asking questions).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes (1) state a specific observation from the tables, (2) include a genuine question connected to the driving question, and (3) are placed under a sensible heading. Look for questions about organising (grouping, averages, graphs), which show progress toward Key Inquiry Question 1, and questions about decisions, which connect to Key Inquiry Question 2. Count how many learners ask about causes and address the need for more data.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add Lesson 2 to the class model of 'How data helps us predict next steps'. The model on the wall is a flow diagram: Raw lists → Ordered lists (Lesson 1) → Frequency tables (Lesson 2) → [Grouped tables, measures, graphs to come] → Interpretation → Next steps for learners and teachers. In groups of 4, learners draw a mini version in their notebooks and add one box or arrow for the frequency table describing what it does (counts how often each score occurs) and what it still cannot do (does not clearly show clusters and spread for a large range of different scores). They write a one-sentence tentative prediction for the next steps for Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku based on evidence so far (for example 'Subject 1: all 20 pass; Subject 2: only 4 of 20 pass, so Subject 2 may need extra support, but we need more information'). They complete the Summary Table: What we observed, What we learned, How we can explain it.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the class model and say: 'Last lesson we added ordered lists. What do we add today, and what does it help with?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups to suggest an addition to the model. Probe: 'What can the frequency table do that the ordered list could not? What can it still not do?' Correct only factual errors (for example if a group says Subject 1 has a mode: 'Check your table. How many scores have f greater than 1?'). Remind learners to treat recommendations as tentative: 'Based on the data so far, what can we say, and what do we still need to find out?' Record the agreed addition on the class model and distribute the Summary Table. Collect the notebooks and tables for review. Optional homework: use the ungrouped table to tally 20 daily mandazi sales for a stall in Mombasa (teacher-provided list) and check that the frequencies add to 20.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with a Summary Table (Observed-Learned-Explained): learners revise a visible model each lesson, connecting new evidence to earlier evidence and to the driving question, so understanding of how data supports decisions grows in steps (NGSS SEP 2, developing and using models).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group's model box (1) states what a frequency table does, (2) names a limitation, and (3) links to the driving question with a cautious prediction. Check that the Summary Table includes accurate details: both tables total 20; Subject 1 all f = 1; Subject 2 has 32 and 60 each with f = 2. Note groups that overstate causes and return to the 'Hypotheses to test' chart.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners built accurate tables, and which needed help with tally grouping or with checking the total of 20? Did the Predict Phase predictions about the number of rows and repeats help learners care about the result, and which predictions changed? How well did learners distinguish what the tables show from why the scores differ? Did anyone claim a cause as a fact, and how did I respond? Did the observation that the Subject 1 table is as long as the list lead learners to the need for a shorter way of organising (Lesson 3)? What will I change about group roles, wait time or cold-calling next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We tallied the 20 scores in Subject 1 and the 20 scores in Subject 2 into frequency tables with columns Score, Tally and Frequency. In Subject 1 every score occurred once (20 different scores). In Subject 2, 32 and 60 each occurred twice and the other scores once (18 different scores). Both frequency columns added to 20.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A frequency distribution table for ungrouped data lists each score, a tally (grouped in fives) and the frequency, and the frequencies must add up to n = 20. Tables help us count accurately and spot repeats, but ungrouped tables with many different scores are long and do not yet clearly show where scores cluster or how widely they spread.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The tables are accurate summaries of how often each score occurs, which helps Madam Achieng, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku check the data. However, Subject 1's table is as long as its list, so we need another way of organising the scores to see patterns and spread. The tables cannot tell us why the subjects differ; that would need more data.

LESSONS.title: Grouped Frequency Distribution Tables: Choosing Class Intervals and Classifying the Scores
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one double lesson of 80 minutes may be used if learners need more time to classify)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: grouped data, class interval, class width, class limits, class boundaries, midpoint, range, tally, frequency, Subject 1, Subject 2

slo.purpose: Learners choose a suitable class width and class limits and classify the scores of Subject 1 and Subject 2 into grouped frequency distribution tables, so that patterns and spread that the raw and ungrouped lists hid become visible and can be used to predict next steps for the learners, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) use the range (28 for Subject 1 and 49 for Subject 2) to decide on a sensible class width; (2) write class intervals with class limits (10-19, 20-29, ..., 90-99) and state class boundaries (9.5-19.5, ..., 89.5-99.5) and midpoints (14.5, 24.5, ..., 94.5); (3) classify data with tally marks and complete a grouped frequency table with frequencies adding to n = 20.
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out investigations (organising and classifying data); analysing and interpreting data (reading clusters and gaps in the grouped table); using mathematics and computational thinking (range, class width, tallying, checking totals); constructing explanations from evidence; communicating findings on manila paper; collaboration in groups of 4.
slo.attitudes: Learners show accuracy and patience when tallying, curiosity about what the grouped data says, respect for others' ideas when groups choose different class widths, and honesty by treating reasons for the score difference as hypotheses and not facts.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD Key Inquiry Questions: 1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? 2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions? Lesson focus: Why does grouping scores into class intervals help us see patterns that 20 separate scores do not?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 2 learners built ungrouped tables with tally marks and saw that every Subject 1 score had frequency 1, and Subject 2 had only 32 and 60 occurring twice. That table was long and showed little. Lesson 3 answers the question 'how can we organise this better?' by grouping. The grouped table (with boundaries and midpoints) is the foundation for Lesson 5 (grouped mean, mode, median), Lesson 6 (histograms and polygons) and Lesson 7 (cumulative frequency and ogives). It also gives the first clear evidence for the driving question: Subject 1 scores cluster between 60 and 99, while Subject 2 scores spread from 10 to 69.
slo.safetyNotes: Low-risk classroom activity. Ensure learners share rulers and manila paper without crowding, keep walkways clear during gallery walk, and use sensitive language: scores belong to Learner 1 to Learner 20 and are not used to label or shame any learner. Remind the class that nothing in the data tells us why scores differ.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng's question remains: what should the learners and the two teachers do next? Learners recall the Lesson 2 ungrouped tables, where Subject 1 had 20 rows each with frequency 1, and predict how many rows a better table should have. Groups use the ranges (28 and 49) to test different class widths (5, 10, 20) on the ascending lists, then agree on a common class width of 10 so both subjects can be compared. They write class limits (10-19 to 90-99), tally all 20 scores of each subject, complete the grouped frequency tables (Subject 1: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 7, 8, 3; Subject 2: 4, 4, 5, 3, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0), check totals of 20, and learn that class boundaries (9.5, 19.5, ..., 99.5) and midpoints (14.5 to 94.5) are needed for later graphs. Learners describe where each subject clusters, add new questions to the Driving Question Board and revise their cumulative model with the grouped evidence, treating reasons for the difference as hypotheses to investigate.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at their Lesson 2 ungrouped tables. Individually (2 minutes) they write a prediction in their notebooks: 'If we group the scores into classes such as 60-69, 70-79, how many rows will the Subject 1 table have, and which classes will have the most learners? What will Subject 2 look like?' They sketch a quick guess of the shape (where the tally marks will pile up). Then they turn to a partner and compare predictions.
framework.teacherMoves: Display on the board: 'Subject 1: every score occurs once. Subject 2: only 32 and 60 occur twice.' Say: 'Madam Achieng does not want a table with 20 rows. How could we squeeze the 20 scores into a few rows and still keep the story?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before anyone speaks. Cold-call 3 learners (not volunteers) to share predictions and record them on a 'Predictions' chart. Ask: 'What do you think will happen to Subject 1's tally marks, and why?' Do not correct predictions yet; say 'We will test this with evidence today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Revisit: committing to a written prediction before instruction makes prior thinking visible and creates a reason to examine the evidence. Comparing with a partner exposes different ideas about what 'grouping' means, which the class will test later in the Explain Phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (a) link the all-frequency-1 problem to the need to group, (b) predict that Subject 1 clusters in high classes and Subject 2 is more spread out, (c) give a reason using the ascending lists. Look for the misconception that grouping 'loses' scores or that classes can overlap. Record on a checklist the names of 5 learners who predicted a number of rows.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (10 min): In groups of 4, learners use the ascending lists and the ranges (Subject 1: 95 - 67 = 28; Subject 2: 60 - 11 = 49). Each group tries a different class width on manila paper (width 5, 10 or 20), counts how many classes are needed, and records advantages and disadvantages. Part B (12 min): The class agrees on one common width of 10 for both subjects, so they can be compared. Groups write the class intervals 10-19, 20-29, ..., 90-99 and tally the scores of Subject 1 and Subject 2 from the ascending lists, ticking each score off. Subject 1 working: 60-69 has 67, 69; 70-79 has 70, 72, 73, 74, 76, 77, 78; 80-89 has 80, 81, 82, 84, 85, 86, 88, 89; 90-99 has 90, 91, 95. Subject 2 working: 10-19: 11, 13, 15, 18; 20-29: 21, 23, 27, 29; 30-39: 30, 31, 32, 32, 35; 40-49: 42, 44, 45; 50-59: 51, 58; 60-69: 60, 60. They complete the frequency columns, remembering tally marks in fives, and check that each total is 20.
framework.teacherMoves: Introduce the idea: 'The range tells us how far the scores stretch. A good class width gives about 5 to 10 classes.' Circulate and ask: 'How many classes would width 5 give for Subject 2? Is that easier to read than 20 rows?' (49 ÷ 5 gives about 10 classes; 49 ÷ 10 gives about 5 to 9 classes.) Prompt: 'Why 10-19 and then 20-29, not 10-20 and 20-30? Where would a score of 20 go?' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 4 groups to report their class widths and number of classes. Guide the whole class to agree on width 10 and the same classes for both subjects 'so we can compare Mr. Otieno's class and Mrs. Wanjiku's class fairly'. Check that classes do not overlap and every score fits in exactly one class. Tell learners to tick each score off the list. Once totals are 20, ask: 'What would it mean if your total was 19 or 21?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Data Collection and Classification (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations): learners compare class widths with evidence, which builds understanding of why class width is a choice that balances detail and readability. Using the same classes for both subjects builds the idea of a fair comparison.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: classes written without gaps or overlaps (10-19, 20-29, ...); tally marks grouped in fives; each score counted once only; frequencies total 20 for both subjects; Subject 1 has zeros for 10-19 to 50-59 and Subject 2 has zeros for 70-79 to 90-99. Common errors: placing 60 in 50-59, counting 32 only once, using classes of unequal width, or totals not equal to 20. Note groups needing help and ask them to recount using the working lists.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners complete the full grouped frequency table for both subjects side by side: class, tally, frequency (Subject 1: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 7, 8, 3; Subject 2: 4, 4, 5, 3, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0; totals 20 and 20). The teacher then introduces class limits, class boundaries and midpoints: for 10-19 the lower boundary is 9.5, the upper is 19.5 and the midpoint is (10 + 19)/2 = 14.5. Groups add boundary and midpoint columns (9.5-19.5 to 89.5-99.5; midpoints 14.5, 24.5, 34.5, 44.5, 54.5, 64.5, 74.5, 84.5, 94.5). Each group writes 3 sentences on manila paper: (1) where Subject 1 scores cluster, (2) where Subject 2 scores cluster and spread, (3) what the grouped table tells Madam Achieng that the raw list did not. They use the language 'may', 'could' and 'we need more data' when suggesting why the subjects differ. Gallery walk: groups read other posters and place a sticky note with 'I agree because...' or 'I wonder...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the two columns of frequencies. Turn and talk: what do you notice?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners. Press for evidence: 'Which class has the most learners in Subject 1? In Subject 2? How many learners in Subject 2 are in classes below 50?' (4 + 4 + 5 + 3 = 16, matching the earlier pass/fail count of 16 below 50.) Ask: 'Why do we need boundaries like 9.5 and 19.5? What gap would a graph have between 19 and 20?' Explain that boundaries close the gap so classes touch, which will be needed for histograms in Lesson 6. Do not teach calculations of mean, median or mode here; say 'those come in Lesson 5'. If a learner suggests a reason such as 'Subject 2 is harder' or 'the teacher is poor', respond: 'That is a hypothesis. What data would we need to test it?' Close with: 'Does the grouped table change your prediction from the start?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Gallery Walk: learners state a claim about each subject's clustering, support it with frequencies from the table, and reason about what it means for next steps. Peer feedback during the gallery walk allows learners to test their reasoning against that of other groups and to separate evidence from speculation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: correct statement that Subject 1 scores are concentrated in 70-79, 80-89 and 90-99 (18 of 20 learners), while Subject 2 scores are spread across six classes from 10-19 to 60-69; correct computation of boundaries and midpoints for at least 3 classes; statements that avoid claiming causes. Exit ticket (2 minutes): 'Write the class, boundaries and midpoint for the score 45, and say how many learners are in that class for Subject 2.' (40-49; 39.5-49.5; midpoint 44.5; frequency 3.) Collect and sort into got it, nearly, not yet.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board: 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' Individually they write on sticky notes (a) one thing the grouped tables helped them understand, and (b) one new question, for example 'What is the average of each grouped table?', 'How can we draw this table as a picture?', 'Why is Subject 2 spread so widely?' or 'Would a second test give the same result?'. Groups place notes under headings such as 'Organising data', 'Summarising data', 'Graphing data' and 'Need more data'. The class marks questions answered by this lesson (for example 'How do we organise 20 scores?') and those to be answered in later lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'What new thing did the grouped table let us see?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking responses, then cold-call 3 learners to read a note aloud and say where it should go. Link notes to future lessons: 'Averages and the middle score come in Lessons 4 and 5, pictures of the table in Lesson 6.' Highlight any question about causes: 'Can this table tell us WHY? What would we need?' Keep a visible list of 'evidence so far': tables show clustering; Subject 1 has 20 of 20 above 60; Subject 2 has 16 below 50. Revisit the KICD question: 'Why is it important to organise data in making decisions?' and ask 2 learners to answer using today's table.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a Tracking Tool: learners see their understanding grow and sort questions by whether they can be answered with the evidence so far. Posting their own questions gives ownership and shows the logic of the sequence, from organising to summarising to graphing to deciding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes reflect understanding (for example, 'grouping makes the clusters visible') and that new questions are mathematical and testable. Count how many learners posted a question about summaries or graphs, which shows readiness for Lessons 4 to 7. Listen for learners who ask about reasons and encourage them to turn the question into data to collect. Note any learner still unsure about class boundaries for a short reteach at the start of Lesson 4.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups update their cumulative model (a poster with 'What we see in the data', 'What we still need to find out' and 'Our prediction for next steps'). They paste or copy the grouped frequency table and add: (1) Subject 1 clusters in 70-89 (15 of 20 learners) with no scores below 60; Subject 2 spreads from 10-19 to 60-69, with 16 of 20 below 50. (2) Revised prediction: Mr. Otieno's class may need extension work; Mrs. Wanjiku's class and the learners may need revision and support, but we need more data (for example topic-by-topic marks and a second test) to find the cause. (3) A sketch of how the grouped table could become a graph. Learners compare with their Predict Phase prediction and write one sentence on what changed. Groups present to another group in 1 minute.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use the grouped table as evidence in your model. What does it add to the ordered list?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Circulate and ask: 'Which class would you tell Madam Achieng to look at first? Why?' and 'Can we say the learners are weak?' Cold-call 3 groups to share one revision to their model. Insist that predictions are evidence-based and that causes are phrased as hypotheses ('may', 'could'). Give feedback on accuracy of frequencies and totals. Preview the next step: 'In Lesson 4 we will calculate the mean, median and mode from the ungrouped scores, so we can describe the centre of each subject with one number.' Keep the posters for Lesson 4.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: learners integrate new evidence (grouped tables showing clustering and spread) into their evolving model of how data supports decisions. Writing what changed from the original prediction builds metacognition and shows how evidence reshapes ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that include correct frequencies for both subjects, mention clustering and spread, link to the pass mark, propose actions for both teachers and the learners, and state what further data are needed. Check that no group claims a cause as a fact. Indicators of mastery: learner can explain why the same classes are used for both subjects, and can state the class, boundaries and midpoint for any given score.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Which learners confused class limits (10-19) with boundaries (9.5-19.5), and which needed to be shown where 20 or 60 belong? Did groups choose class width 10 for good reasons from the range, or just because it was suggested? Were tally counts accurate, and did every total reach 20? How many learners avoided stating causes as facts? Which questions on the Driving Question Board show readiness for the mean, median and mode in Lessons 4 and 5, and for graphs in Lessons 6 and 7? What would you change next time, for example more time for classifying or a shorter gallery walk?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We organised the 20 scores of Subject 1 and Subject 2 into grouped frequency tables using a common class width of 10 (classes 10-19 to 90-99). Subject 1 frequencies: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 7, 8, 3 and Subject 2 frequencies: 4, 4, 5, 3, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, each totalling 20.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned how to use the range (28 and 49) to choose a class width, write class limits, find class boundaries (9.5, 19.5, ..., 99.5) and midpoints (14.5, ..., 94.5), and classify scores with tally marks so that frequencies add to n = 20.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Grouping shows that Subject 1 scores cluster high (70-89 has 15 of 20 learners and no score is below 60), while Subject 2 scores are spread out (16 of 20 are below 50). The raw lists hid this pattern. The tables do not tell us why, so we need more data, such as topic-by-topic marks and a second test, before deciding the causes and next steps.

LESSONS.title: Mean, Mode and Median of Ungrouped Data: Comparing the Two Subjects
LESSONS.aresKeywords: mean, median, mode, no mode, bimodal, measure of central tendency, ungrouped data, sum, ordered list, typical value, outlier, spread

slo.purpose: To help learners calculate and interpret the mean, mode and median of the ungrouped scores in Subject 1 and Subject 2, and use these single typical values to compare the two subjects and move closer to answering how the data can predict next steps.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) calculate the mean as sum of x divided by n (Subject 1: 1607/20 = 80.35; Subject 2: 677/20 = 33.85); (2) find the median as the average of the 10th and 11th ordered values (Subject 1: (80+81)/2 = 80.5; Subject 2: (31+32)/2 = 31.5); (3) find the mode from the ungrouped frequencies, including the no-mode case (Subject 1) and the bimodal case (Subject 2: 32 and 60); (4) interpret each measure in the context of the two subjects.
slo.skills: Calculating, ordering and counting data; analysing and interpreting data (NGSS-style practice: analysing and interpreting data); using mathematics and computational thinking; constructing explanations from evidence; communicating findings on manila paper; working collaboratively in groups of 4.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about what numbers tell us; honesty and accuracy when calculating; respect for others' ideas during group discussion; caution in drawing conclusions (using words like 'may', 'could' and 'we need more data'); appreciation of data in making decisions.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? 2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-3 showed that raw lists are hard to read: Lesson 1 ordered the scores and counted passes (20 pass in Subject 1; 4 pass and 16 fail in Subject 2), Lesson 2 built ungrouped frequency tables, and Lesson 3 grouped the data. Lesson 4 now summarises each whole set with ONE typical value (mean, median, mode). These exact values give the evidence that Lesson 5 will estimate again from grouped data, and that Lessons 6-7 will compare with graphs. This lesson gives learners their first numeric answer to: do the two subjects differ in their typical score, and what might Madam Achieng, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku do next?
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Learners use pencils, rulers, manila paper and calculators (or manual long addition). Keep walkways clear when groups display manila paper. Remind learners to treat the scores as class data and not to tease any individual learner about their marks (Learner 1 to Learner 20 are used instead of names).

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng has asked the Grade 10 class at a day secondary school in Kisumu to use the scores of the same 20 learners in Subject 1 (Mr. Otieno) and Subject 2 (Mrs. Wanjiku) to decide next steps. In earlier lessons learners ordered the scores, counted passes and built frequency tables. In this lesson, groups of 4 predict which subject has the higher typical score, then calculate the mean, median and mode of each set from the ordered lists and ungrouped frequency tables. They discover that Subject 1 has mean 80.35, median 80.5 and no mode, while Subject 2 has mean 33.85, median 31.5 and two modes (32 and 60). They interpret what each measure says, compare the two subjects, and note what the measures cannot tell them (such as WHY the scores differ or how spread out they are). The Driving Question Board and the class model are updated with this new evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the puzzle: the same 20 learners scored 67 to 95 in Subject 1 but 11 to 60 in Subject 2. Each learner individually writes on a sticky note or in the exercise book: (a) 'If we had to choose ONE number to describe the whole class in Subject 1 and ONE for Subject 2, what would the numbers be, roughly?' (b) 'Will the one number for Subject 2 be above or below 50? Why?' Then in groups of 4 they share and agree on a group prediction, writing it on manila paper. They also predict: 'Will Subject 1 have a score that appears most often? Will Subject 2?' using the ascending lists from Lesson 1 displayed on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the two ascending lists (Subject 1: 67, 69, 70, 72, 73, 74, 76, 77, 78, 80, 81, 82, 84, 85, 86, 88, 89, 90, 91, 95; Subject 2: 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 23, 27, 29, 30, 31, 32, 32, 35, 42, 44, 45, 51, 58, 60, 60). Say: 'Madam Achieng cannot read 40 numbers every time she makes a decision. What single number could stand for each subject?' Give 2 minutes of silent individual writing. WAIT TIME: after asking 'Will the typical score in Subject 2 be above or below the pass mark of 50?' wait 10-15 seconds before taking responses. Cold-call 4 groups to share predictions; record ALL predictions on the board without judging. Ask: 'What in the lists made you choose that number?' Do not say whether predictions are right.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain): Learners commit to a prediction and justify it with evidence from the ordered lists. This surfaces the idea that 'typical' could mean the middle, the most common or the 'fair share' value, and creates a need for the three measures. Learners later check predictions against calculations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners (1) refer to the lists when justifying predictions, (2) use words like 'middle', 'most common' or 'average' for 'typical', and (3) predict Subject 1 higher than Subject 2. Tally on a clipboard how many groups predict a Subject 2 typical value below 50. Note misconceptions such as 'the typical score is the highest score' or 'mean is always the middle value'.

framework.learnerExperience: Station-style group investigation (groups of 4, each learner takes a role: reader, recorder, calculator, checker). Part A (MODE): Using the ungrouped frequency tables from Lesson 2, groups identify the score with the highest frequency. Subject 1: every score occurs once, so they must decide what that means (no mode). Subject 2: 32 and 60 each occur twice (bimodal). Part B (MEDIAN): Using the ascending lists, groups count to the 10th and 11th values, since n = 20 is even. Subject 1: 10th = 80, 11th = 81, median = (80+81)/2 = 80.5. Subject 2: 10th = 31, 11th = 32, median = 31.5. They cross-check by counting 10 values on each side. Part C (MEAN): Groups add all 20 scores in each subject (Subject 1 sum = 1607; Subject 2 sum = 677), then divide by 20: mean = 80.35 for Subject 1 and 33.85 for Subject 2. Groups record x, sum of x and n in a results table on manila paper, and compare with their predictions.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Pose: 'Where in the table do you look to find the mode? What does a frequency of 1 for every score tell you?' For the median ask: 'Why do we need two middle values when n = 20? Show me with your pencil which are the 10th and 11th.' For the mean: 'Add in pairs or tens to reduce errors; check your sum with your partner. What should the sums be close to?' Provide a quick check: if a group's Subject 1 sum is not 1607 or Subject 2 sum is not 677, say 'Recheck the addition in two halves: first ten scores, then last ten'. WAIT TIME: after asking 'Can a data set have no mode? Two modes?' wait 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners from different groups. Remind them to keep the Learner 1 to Learner 20 order only for the raw lists, not for the ordered lists. Use the Kenyan side example (mandazi sales in Mombasa: 20, 25, 25, 30, 40 mandazi, mean 28) briefly to show mean as 'fair share' if learners struggle.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection and cross-checking (Analysing and Interpreting Data): Learners calculate the three measures using three different representations (frequency table, ordered list, sum), then verify each result by a second method. This builds understanding that the measures describe the SAME data in different ways and that checking guards against errors.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) learners correctly identify the 10th and 11th values and average them; (2) learners state 'no mode' for Subject 1 rather than writing 0 or 80; (3) learners write both 32 and 60 as modes; (4) sums 1607 and 677 and means 80.35 and 33.85 appear on manila paper, with answers rounded to 2 dp. Use a thumbs-up/down check: 'Thumbs up if you got a sum of 1607 for Subject 1'. Note groups needing support with division by 20 and give a mini-conference.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups use their results to build a comparison table (Measure | Subject 1 | Subject 2): mean 80.35 | 33.85; median 80.5 | 31.5; mode none | 32 and 60. Then they write explanations answering: (1) 'What does the mean of 80.35 tell us about Subject 1 and the mean of 33.85 about Subject 2 compared with the pass mark of 50?' (2) 'Why are the mean and median close in Subject 1 and also close in Subject 2? What would happen to the mean if Learner 14, who scored 11 in Subject 2, had scored 51?' (3) 'Which measure is most useful for Madam Achieng? Why is the mode less useful here?' (4) 'What can these three numbers NOT tell us?' Learners should note that they cannot say WHY the scores differ (test difficulty, teaching method and revision time are unknown) and that the measures do not show spread (the range 28 versus 49 from Lesson 1 is still needed). Groups share explanations in a gallery walk, leaving one question on a sticky note for another group.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use evidence from your table: because the Subject 1 mean is 80.35, we can say...' Provide sentence starters: 'The typical score in Subject 1 is higher than in Subject 2 because...', 'This may mean... but we need more data about...'. Ask the 'what if' question about changing one score and give 15 seconds of WAIT TIME before cold-calling 3 learners; guide them to see that one extreme score moves the mean by 40/20 = 2 marks while the median stays near the middle. Probe: 'Does a higher mean show that Mr. Otieno teaches better than Mrs. Wanjiku? What would we need to know?' Correct any causal claims by asking: 'Is that a fact from the data or a hypothesis to investigate?' Facilitate the gallery walk (5 minutes), asking each group to leave 1 'I wonder' sticky note. Do NOT introduce grouped-data formulas (Lesson 5), histograms (Lesson 6) or quartiles (Lessons 7-8).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a Gallery Walk: Learners make a claim about the subjects, support it with the calculated measures, and reason about what the measures show and hide. Peer review during the gallery walk exposes different interpretations and builds the habit of caution about causes (hypotheses, not facts).
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for explanations that (1) cite specific numbers (80.35, 33.85, 80.5, 31.5) rather than 'higher' only; (2) compare to the pass mark of 50; (3) use cautious language ('may', 'could', 'we need more data'); (4) recognise that mean and median can both describe the centre but may differ with extreme scores. Use an exit-style question on a half sheet: 'Write one sentence comparing the typical score in the two subjects and one thing the typical score cannot tell us.' Sort responses into: accurate, partly accurate, needs reteaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board with the question: 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' In groups they (a) place sticky notes showing what they now KNOW (for example, 'Typical score in Subject 1 is about 80 and in Subject 2 about 32-34', 'Mean and median are close in each subject', 'Subject 1 has no mode and Subject 2 has two modes'), (b) add new questions (for example, 'Why are the Subject 2 scores so much lower for the same learners?', 'How spread out are the scores around the mean?', 'Can we show this on a graph?', 'Do the 16 learners below 50 need remedial support?'), and (c) move earlier questions that are now partly answered. They link questions to the two KICD inquiry questions.
framework.teacherMoves: Read the Driving Question aloud, then say: 'Look at the board. What have we found out today that helps with next steps? What new questions do we have?' Give 1 minute of silent writing and WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before asking for volunteers. Cold-call 3 groups to place and justify notes. Sort questions into categories on the board: 'Spread', 'Graphs', 'Causes (need more data)', 'Actions'. Mark questions Lesson 5 (grouped estimates), Lesson 6-7 (graphs) or Lesson 8 (interpretation) will address. Highlight that the question about causes cannot be answered from these scores alone and may need topic-by-topic marks or a second test, as Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku might plan.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of learning: Learners track what they know, what they still wonder, and where they will look next. This makes progress visible and keeps the sequence of lessons purposeful, linking each calculation back to the decision Madam Achieng must make.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that sticky notes include at least one evidence-based statement with a number from the lesson and at least one new question about spread, causes or action. Observe whether learners place notes in the right category. Count the groups able to link a question to a future lesson. Record learners who only write vague questions ('Why?') and prompt with 'Why what? Which number made you wonder?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update the class model (a large poster showing the pathway from raw data to decision). In groups they add a new layer labelled 'Summarise with one typical value' showing: raw scores -> ordered list -> frequency table -> grouped table -> mean, median, mode -> (coming next: graphs and spread) -> comparison -> next steps. Beside it they write the key findings: Subject 1: mean 80.35, median 80.5, no mode; Subject 2: mean 33.85, median 31.5, modes 32 and 60. They add a first tentative prediction for next steps, labelled as a hypothesis: for example, 'Subject 1 learners are passing at a typical level well above 50; Subject 2 typical score is below 50, so revision may be needed, but we need more data to know why.' Each learner completes a personal 'What I observed / What I learned / How I can explain it' entry for the Summary Table.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Show on the model where today's work fits. What new arrow or box do we need?' Ask: 'What does the model still NOT explain?' (spread, shape, causes). Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to read their entries. Guide learners to word predictions cautiously: 'Mr. Otieno's class may continue with extension work; Mrs. Wanjiku and the class may need to revise Subject 2 topics; we need more data to find the cause.' Do not give final recommendations; those are developed in Lessons 8-9. Collect Summary Table entries for review. Set a short take-home task: find the mean of five daily mandazi sales or tea-picking weights from a local context to practise the method.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: Learners add the new evidence to a shared model and identify gaps, so each lesson builds on the last. Writing tentative predictions as hypotheses develops scientific habits of caution and evidence-based reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that the model includes the correct values (80.35, 80.5, none; 33.85, 31.5, 32 and 60) and that the predictions use cautious language. Observable indicators: learners can explain in their own words what mean, median and mode each tell us, and name one limitation (no information about spread or causes). Review Summary Table entries for accuracy, and note learners to support in the next lesson on grouped data.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson reflect: (1) Did every group correctly use the 10th and 11th values for the median and write 'no mode' and 'bimodal' correctly? Which learners confused no mode with a mode of zero? (2) Did learners use cautious language when interpreting the difference between subjects, or did they claim causes such as 'Mr. Otieno teaches better'? How did I respond? (3) How well did learners connect the measures to the pass mark of 50 and to Madam Achieng's decision? (4) Which addition or division errors were most common, and should I provide a quick calculation routine before Lesson 5? (5) Which DQB questions about spread and graphs will drive the next lessons, and did learners notice that mean and median alone do not show how spread out the scores are? (6) Were wait time and cold-calling used evenly so quieter learners contributed?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Calculating from the ordered lists and frequency tables, we observed that Subject 1 has a sum of 1607, mean 80.35, median 80.5 and no mode, while Subject 2 has a sum of 677, mean 33.85, median 31.5 and two modes (32 and 60).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned how to calculate the mean (sum of x divided by n), the median (average of the 10th and 11th ordered values when n = 20) and the mode (the most frequent score, which may be none or more than one), and that each gives a different way to describe a typical score.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The typical score in Subject 1 (about 80) is well above the pass mark of 50, while the typical score in Subject 2 (about 32-34) is below it, so the difference seems to be between subjects and not because the learners are weak overall; the measures may help predict next steps but they do not show spread or the cause, so we need more data.
