LESSONS.title: Mean, Mode and Median of Grouped Data: Estimating the Centre of Each Subject
LESSONS.aresKeywords: grouped data, class midpoint, fx, estimated mean, modal class, estimated mode, median class, estimated median, class boundary, cumulative frequency, estimate

slo.purpose: Learners estimate the mean, mode and median of Subject 1 and Subject 2 from the grouped frequency tables, compare the estimates with the exact ungrouped values from Lesson 4, and explain why grouped measures are only estimates. This moves the class closer to Madam Achieng's request to predict next steps for the learners, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (1) the estimated mean of grouped data = sum of fx / sum of f, using class midpoints x; (2) the modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the mode is estimated by L + (d1/(d1+d2)) x w; (3) the median class contains the (n/2)th value, and the median is estimated by L + ((n/2 - cf)/f) x w; (4) grouped measures are estimates because individual scores are replaced by midpoints or positions within classes, so they differ slightly from exact values (Subject 1 exact mean 80.35, median 80.5; Subject 2 exact mean 33.85, median 31.5).
slo.skills: Learners will: calculate midpoints and fx; sum fx and divide by n = 20; identify modal and median classes; apply the mode and median formulas with class boundaries; compare estimates with the exact values; communicate results in a comparison table. Science and Engineering Practices (adapted for Mathematics): Analysing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Constructing Explanations; Engaging in Argument from Evidence.
slo.attitudes: Learners will show accuracy and patience when working with several steps, honesty in reporting estimates as estimates, curiosity about why two subjects differ, respect for others' methods in groups of 4, and caution in not claiming reasons for the score difference without more data.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 3 gave us the grouped tables with boundaries and midpoints. Lesson 4 gave us the exact mean, median and mode from the ungrouped lists. In Lesson 5 learners use only the grouped tables to estimate the same measures, and learn how close the estimates are. These estimates give the centre of each subject (about 80 versus about 34) and prepare for Lesson 6 (histograms and frequency polygons, using the modal class and midpoints) and Lesson 7 (ogives, with the grouped median formula as a check).
slo.safetyNotes: Low-risk classroom lesson. Learners work on desks and manila paper; keep walkways clear. Remind learners that the marks belong to Learner 1 to Learner 20 and that scores should not be used to tease anyone. Groups of 4 should share tasks fairly so that every member calculates.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng, the Deputy Principal of a day secondary school in Kisumu, asked the class to use the scores of the same 20 learners in Subject 1 (Mr. Otieno) and Subject 2 (Mrs. Wanjiku) to decide next steps. In Lessons 1-4 learners ordered the scores, built tables and found exact measures. Today they work only from the grouped tables (classes 10-19 to 90-99) to estimate the mean, modal class and mode, and median. They predict how close grouped estimates will be to the exact values, calculate them step by step, and compare. The estimates (means 80.5 and 35; modes 81.2 and 32.8; medians 80.75 and 33.5) agree closely with the exact values, so the picture is clear: Subject 1 is high, and Subject 2 is low. Learners also see why the numbers are estimates. The lesson ends by adding the estimates to the Driving Question Board and to the class model. We still do not know WHY the scores differ; reasons remain hypotheses to investigate.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the grouped frequency table from Lesson 3 (classes 10-19 to 90-99 for both subjects) and the exact measures from Lesson 4 (Subject 1 mean 80.35, median 80.5, no mode; Subject 2 mean 33.85, median 31.5, modes 32 and 60). Individually they write: 'If Madam Achieng only gave us the grouped table and not the 20 scores, could we still find the mean, mode and median? Would they be exactly the same? Predict the grouped mean for each subject.' They record a prediction on a sticky note or in their books (e.g. 'about 80 for Subject 1 and about 35 for Subject 2') with a reason, then share with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the grouped table on the board (Subject 1 frequencies 0,0,0,0,0,2,7,8,3; Subject 2 frequencies 4,4,5,3,2,2,0,0,0). Say: 'Imagine the 20 scores are lost and only this table survives. Can we still say where the centre of each subject is?' Give 1 minute silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before any talk. Pair-share for 2 minutes. Cold-call 4 learners: 'What do you predict for Subject 1? For Subject 2? Why?' Ask 2 more: 'Will it match 80.35 and 33.85 exactly?' Record predictions on the board without judging them. Say: 'We will test your predictions with evidence today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with a Prediction Gallery: committing to a numerical prediction before calculation creates a reason to calculate and exposes the idea that a table hides individual scores. Learners compare their predictions with results later, which builds understanding of why estimates occur.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe: (1) Do predictions place Subject 1 near the 70s-80s and Subject 2 near the 30s-40s using the table? (2) Do learners give a reason (e.g. 'most scores are in 80-89') rather than a guess? (3) Do at least 5 learners say the answers may not be exactly equal to Lesson 4's values? Note learners who think grouping loses no information and revisit this in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A: Estimated mean. In groups of 4 learners copy the grouped table and add columns x (midpoint: 14.5, 24.5, 34.5, 44.5, 54.5, 64.5, 74.5, 84.5, 94.5) and fx. For Subject 1 they calculate 2(64.5)+7(74.5)+8(84.5)+3(94.5) = 129+521.5+676+283.5 = 1610 and mean = 1610/20 = 80.5. For Subject 2 they calculate 4(14.5)+4(24.5)+5(34.5)+3(44.5)+2(54.5)+2(64.5) = 58+98+172.5+133.5+109+129 = 700 and mean = 700/20 = 35. Part B: Modal class and mode. They find the modal classes (Subject 1: 80-89, f = 8; Subject 2: 30-39, f = 5), then use boundaries: Subject 1: L = 79.5, d1 = 8-7 = 1, d2 = 8-3 = 5, mode = 79.5 + (1/6)(10) = 81.2; Subject 2: L = 29.5, d1 = 5-4 = 1, d2 = 5-3 = 2, mode = 29.5 + (1/3)(10) = 32.8. Part C: Median. They build a cumulative frequency column (Subject 1: 0,0,0,0,0,2,9,17,20; Subject 2: 4,8,13,16,18,20,20,20,20), find the 10th position (n/2 = 10), the median class (Subject 1: 80-89 with cf before = 9, f = 8; Subject 2: 30-39 with cf before = 8, f = 5), and calculate: Subject 1 = 79.5 + (1/8)(10) = 80.75; Subject 2 = 29.5 + (2/5)(10) = 33.5. Learners complete a comparison table: grouped estimate versus exact value from Lesson 4.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Launch with: 'Why do we use the midpoint of 60-69 as 64.5 and not 67 or 69?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 2 groups. Model ONE row (Subject 1, class 70-79: 7 x 74.5 = 521.5) on the board, then let groups continue. Prompt: 'What does the sum of f have to be? Check it equals 20 before you go on.' For the mode, say: 'Which class is tallest? What are the classes before and after it? Write d1 and d2 BEFORE you substitute.' For the median say: 'The median is the 10th value. How many learners are below 79.5? Then how far into the 80-89 class do we need to go?' Cold-call 3 learners to give the median class and cf. Stop each group at the end of each part to check answers (1610, 700; 81.2, 32.8; 80.75, 33.5) before moving on. Point out that zero-frequency classes contribute fx = 0 but are still in the table. Extension question: 'If the class width were 5, would the estimates change?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Data Analysis with a Worked Example and Think-Aloud: one modelled row followed by learner calculations lets learners see the procedure and then own it. Comparing grouped estimates with exact Lesson 4 values builds a sense of accuracy and develops the concept of 'estimate'.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check: (1) midpoints written correctly for all 9 classes; (2) sum of fx = 1610 and 700 and divided by 20 (not by 9, the number of classes); (3) correct boundaries used (79.5 and 29.5), not limits (80 and 30); (4) d1 and d2 identified correctly; (5) correct cf before the median class (9 and 8). Common errors to note: dividing by the number of classes; using the class limit instead of the boundary; using cf of the median class instead of the cf before it; confusing the modal class with the mode. Collect one group's table as a quick check.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups complete a comparison table: Measure | Subject 1 exact (Lesson 4) | Subject 1 grouped estimate | Subject 2 exact | Subject 2 grouped estimate. Mean: 80.35 / 80.5; 33.85 / 35. Median: 80.5 / 80.75; 31.5 / 33.5. Mode: none / 81.2 (modal class 80-89); 32 and 60 / 32.8 (modal class 30-39). They then discuss: (a) Which estimates are close to the exact values? (b) Why are they not exactly equal? (e.g. grouping replaces each score with the midpoint of its class; the actual scores in 80-89 range from 80 to 89 and average 84.1, not 84.5; the formulas assume scores are evenly spread within the class). (c) Subject 1 has no exact mode, yet the grouped table gives a modal class and mode estimate. What does this tell us? (d) What do the estimates say about the two subjects and what could Madam Achieng predict? Each group writes a 2-3 sentence claim-evidence-reasoning statement on manila paper, e.g. 'Subject 1 estimated mean 80.5 is much higher than Subject 2 estimated mean 35, so the typical learner scores far higher in Subject 1. We need more data to find out why.'
framework.teacherMoves: Pose: 'Is 80.5 a better or worse answer than 80.35? Which one is exact?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Press for reasoning: 'Say that again using the words midpoint and class.' Guide a mini-demonstration: Subject 1 class 60-69 holds scores 67 and 69, but we treated them as 64.5 and 64.5. 'Who is that unfair to? Who is helped?' Then ask: 'Would it change the decision if the mean were 80.35 or 80.5?' (No: both show all learners well above 50.) Challenge a misconception: 'Someone said the grouped mean is wrong. Is it wrong or an estimate?' Ask 4 cold-call learners to read out their claim statements. Insist on cautious language: 'Can we say Mrs. Wanjiku taught badly? What do we actually know? What do we NOT know?' Record: 'Estimates close to exact values; difference between subjects is clear; reasons unknown, so we need more data.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Error Analysis: learners state a claim (the estimates compare well and show a big gap), cite the numbers as evidence, and reason about how grouping causes small differences. This builds a deeper understanding of estimation and develops statistical caution about causes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners say estimates differ because midpoints and position formulas stand in for actual scores; (2) learners do not say the estimates are mistakes; (3) CER statements cite at least two numbers (e.g. 80.5 and 35); (4) statements avoid claiming causes and use 'may', 'could' or 'we need more data'; (5) learners state that the grouped values lead to the same conclusion as the exact values. Use a thumbs-up/sideways/down check on: 'I can explain why grouped measures are estimates.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board: 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' On sticky notes they add (a) one thing they now know, e.g. 'The estimated means are 80.5 and 35, so Subject 1 is much higher' and (b) one new question, e.g. 'Can a graph show the spread better than these measures?', 'Both subjects are centred differently, but is one more spread out?', 'Why did the same learners do so well in one subject and so poorly in the other?', 'Does the mean hide the 16 learners below 50?' They place notes under headings: Answered / Partly answered / New questions. Groups link at least one note to the Key Inquiry Questions on organising data with tables and on why collecting, organising and interpreting data matters for decisions.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. What has today's evidence added to our answer for Madam Achieng?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to read a new note aloud and say which earlier note it connects to. Cluster questions on the board: 'centre', 'spread', 'causes', 'graphs', 'action'. Point out: 'Questions about spread and shape need graphs, which we will draw in Lesson 6 and 7. Questions about why need new data, which we will plan in Lesson 9.' Move the question 'Are the grouped values the same as the exact ones?' to 'Answered: close, but estimates'. Keep any claim about causes under 'Questions to investigate'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with Question Clustering: externalising what is known and not yet known keeps the investigation learner-driven, connects today's calculation to the anchoring phenomenon, and shows how the next lessons (graphs and quartiles) respond to learners' own questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check: (1) at least one note per learner cites a specific number from today (80.5, 35, 81.2, 32.8, 80.75, 33.5); (2) questions are genuine and linked to the phenomenon (spread, graphs, causes, action); (3) at least 3 groups raise a question about spread or the 16 learners below 50; (4) no note states a cause as a fact. Record themes to adjust Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model for the driving question, using a summary table on manila paper with columns: Subject | Estimated mean | Modal class / estimated mode | Median estimate | Prediction (cautious). Subject 1: 80.5 | 80-89 / 81.2 | 80.75 | 'Scores are high around the 80s; all learners are likely to pass again; extension work could be given.' Subject 2: 35 | 30-39 / 32.8 | 33.5 | 'Typical score is in the 30s, below the pass mark of 50; revision and remedial support are likely needed; we need more data (topic-by-topic marks, a second test) to find causes.' Learners add a line: 'Grouped measures are estimates and differ slightly from the exact values (80.35, 33.85; 80.5, 31.5).' Each group adds one 'What we still need' arrow: 'spread picture (graphs, Lesson 6 and 7)'. Learners then complete a quick exit ticket: 'Calculate the estimated mean for a small table and say why it is an estimate.' Optional side example: daily mandazi sales in Mombasa grouped in classes of 10 (this is a practice context only and does not change the anchor data).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Let us add today's evidence to our model for Madam Achieng. What is the typical score in each subject?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to complete the table cells orally before groups write. Ask: 'Which measure would you give to Madam Achieng first, and why?' Prompt careful predictions: 'Which words show we are not sure of the cause: may, could, or must?' Ask 2 groups to present their table on manila paper; require them to name one strength and one limitation of grouped estimates. Use the exit ticket to sort learners into 'secure' (all steps correct), 'nearly' (one slip), and 'not yet', and plan a short revisit for the last group. Preview: 'Next lesson we draw histograms and frequency polygons to SEE these two subjects side by side, using the same classes and scales.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Gallery Walk: updating the shared model with new evidence from the grouped measures shows how understanding builds lesson by lesson. Writing a cautious prediction trains learners to separate what the data show (centre, gap) from what they do not show (causes).
framework.formativeAssessment: Success looks like: (1) tables carry correct values (80.5, 35; 80-89 and 30-39; 81.2 and 32.8; 80.75 and 33.5); (2) predictions are tied to numbers and the pass mark of 50; (3) learners use 'estimate' for grouped values; (4) hypotheses are separate from facts; (5) the exit ticket shows correct midpoints, fx and division by n. Target at least 15 of 20 learners secure on the estimated mean; follow up with a small group on the median formula if more than 5 learners misuse cf.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Reflect after the lesson: (1) Did learners divide sum of fx by n = 20 rather than by 9 classes? (2) How many used boundaries (79.5, 29.5) correctly in the mode and median formulas? (3) Could learners explain why 80.5 and 80.35 differ without saying one is wrong? (4) Did any learner or group claim a cause for the difference between Subject 1 and Subject 2? How did I respond? (5) Which questions on the DQB point to spread and graphs, and how will I use them to launch Lesson 6? (6) Which learners need extra practice with cumulative frequency before the ogive work in Lesson 7? Consider whether pacing across the two 40-minute periods allowed enough time for Part C (median).

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the grouped tables let us estimate the mean (Subject 1: 1610/20 = 80.5; Subject 2: 700/20 = 35), the modal class and mode (80-89, about 81.2; 30-39, about 32.8) and the median (about 80.75 and 33.5). These are close to the exact values from Lesson 4 but not identical.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned how to use midpoints and fx to estimate the mean, boundaries and d1, d2 to estimate the mode, and cumulative frequency to estimate the median. We learned that grouped measures are estimates because each score is replaced by its class midpoint or position in the class.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that Subject 1 is centred around 80 and Subject 2 around 34, so decisions must be made per subject: the same learners cannot all be 'weak'. We cannot yet say why the scores differ, and we need spread information and more data before deciding the full next steps.

LESSONS.title: Representation of Data I: Histograms and Frequency Polygons
LESSONS.aresKeywords: histogram, frequency polygon, class boundaries, midpoint, frequency, shape, spread, modal class, same axes

slo.purpose: To draw a histogram using class boundaries and a frequency polygon using class midpoints for Subject 1 and Subject 2, and to read the shape and spread of each subject from the graphs.
slo.knowledge: Learners draw a histogram with touching bars at the class boundaries (9.5 to 99.5) with frequency on the vertical axis. They draw a frequency polygon by plotting (midpoint, frequency) points at 14.5, 24.5, ..., 94.5 and joining them with straight lines, closing to the axis at the empty classes either side. They know both graphs must use the same classes and the same axis scales so that the two subjects can be compared.
slo.skills: Drawing and labelling graphs accurately on graph paper; reading the grouped frequency table; choosing a scale; describing shape (clustered or spread out), modal class and spread; comparing two graphs; communicating findings on manila paper (groups of 4). Science and Engineering Practices: analysing and interpreting data, using mathematics, constructing explanations.
slo.attitudes: Accuracy and neatness in drawing; curiosity about what a picture of data shows; respect for others' ideas during groupwork; honesty in not claiming causes the data cannot show.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? 2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 5 ordered the scores, built ungrouped and grouped tables, and calculated mean, mode and median. Lesson 6 turns the grouped table into pictures so that the shape and spread that the raw lists hid become visible. It prepares for Lesson 7 (cumulative frequency and ogives), which will reuse the graph-drawing skills, and Lesson 8 (comparing subjects and predicting next steps).
slo.safetyNotes: Learners use sharp pencils, rulers and compasses/dividers carefully. Keep bags and walkways clear in the classroom. Groups pass manila paper and markers carefully and keep the floor free to prevent trips.

LESSONS.overview: Back at the Grade 10 class in Kisumu, Madam Achieng still wants to know what to do about Mr. Otieno's Subject 1 and Mrs. Wanjiku's Subject 2. Learners have a grouped frequency table (common class width 10, classes 10-19 to 90-99, n = 20 for both subjects) and know the grouped means 80.5 and 35 and the modal classes 80-89 and 30-39. In this lesson they turn the table into a histogram and a frequency polygon for each subject on the same axes. They see that Subject 1 is a tight block of bars between 60 and 99, while Subject 2 is spread across 10 to 69 and sits much further left. Learners make claims from the pictures, but treat reasons for the difference as hypotheses to investigate and not as facts, because the data cannot tell us why.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the grouped frequency table for both subjects (classes 10-19 to 90-99; Subject 1: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 7, 8, 3; Subject 2: 4, 4, 5, 3, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0). Individually, for 3 minutes, they sketch what they think a bar graph of each subject would look like (where the tall bars will be, how wide the picture is) and write one sentence: 'I think the Subject 1 picture will look ___ and the Subject 2 picture will look ___ because ___.' They then share with a partner and the pair decides which subject will look more spread out.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the table on the board. Say: 'Madam Achieng cannot read 40 numbers quickly. Before we draw anything, sketch what you expect each subject to look like.' Give 3 minutes of silent sketching. Then ask: 'Which subject will have its tallest bar on the right side of the graph, and why?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners, including at least 2 who did not volunteer. Ask each: 'What in the table makes you say that?' Record 2 or 3 predictions on the board without judging them. Ask: 'How will we know if your sketch is right?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with Think-Pair-Share: committing to a prediction from the table first exposes learners' ideas about shape and spread. Later comparison of the drawn graphs with their sketches creates cognitive conflict or confirmation, which builds understanding of how a graph summarises a frequency table.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: sketches that place the Subject 1 tall bars on the right and the Subject 2 bars on the left (correct use of the table); learners who refer to frequencies such as 8 in 80-89 or 5 in 30-39; learners who say a graph will show 'spread' without defining it. Note learners who sketch the bars with gaps or draw 20 separate bars, which shows they have not linked the table classes to a graph. Tick on a class list those who give a justified prediction.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners draw on graph paper: (1) a histogram for Subject 1 and a histogram for Subject 2, using the same horizontal scale (class boundaries 9.5, 19.5, ..., 99.5) and the same vertical scale (frequency 0 to 8). The bars touch, are drawn at the class boundaries, and the classes with frequency 0 have no height. (2) A frequency polygon for each subject on the same axes: they find the midpoints 14.5, 24.5, 34.5, 44.5, 54.5, 64.5, 74.5, 84.5, 94.5, plot (midpoint, frequency) points, join with straight lines and close the polygon to the axis at the empty classes on either side (4.5 and 104.5). Roles: scribe, plotter, checker (checks the boundaries and frequency against the table), reporter. Learners check that bar heights add to 20 for each subject. Each group draws both polygons on one pair of axes in two colours to compare.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first bar only: 'The class 10-19 really starts at 9.5 and ends at 19.5 because scores are whole numbers and the bars must touch. Where does the bar for 20-29 start?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Circulate and ask: 'Why is there no bar for 50-59 in Subject 1?' and 'What is the midpoint of 60-69 and why do we plot it there?' Prompt: 'What is the sum of your heights? It must be 20.' For groups that finish early: 'Where do you put the first and last point of the polygon, and why do we close it to the axis?' Stop at 25 minutes for a gallery walk of 5 minutes where groups compare their graphs to the manila paper of another group and fix errors. Remind: 'Same scales for both subjects, or the comparison is not fair.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery Walk with Peer Checking: learners compare their drawn graphs with those of other groups, using a checklist (touching bars, boundaries, midpoints, equal scales, title and labels). This builds understanding through noticing and correcting the connections between the grouped table, class boundaries and midpoints from Lessons 3 and 5.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: bars drawn from 9.5 to 19.5 and so on (not 10 to 19) with no gaps; frequency (not score) on the vertical axis; heights of Subject 1 bars 2, 7, 8, 3 from 59.5 to 99.5 and Subject 2 bars 4, 4, 5, 3, 2, 2 from 9.5 to 69.5; polygon points at the midpoints and closed at the axis; the same scale on both graphs. Use a checklist to mark each group. Common errors to note: gaps between bars, plotting the polygon at class limits (like 10 or 19), wrong closing, and using different scales.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group uses its two graphs to write on manila paper a short report for Madam Achieng, answering: (a) Where is the tallest bar (modal class) in each subject? (b) Which subject is more spread out and how do you know from the graph? (c) Which polygon is further to the right? What does this suggest about the scores? (d) What can the graphs NOT tell us (for example why the scores differ)? Learners compare these findings with their Predict sketches and explain any differences. Expected findings: Subject 1 modal class 80-89 (f = 8), scores clustered between 60 and 99, range 28; Subject 2 modal class 30-39 (f = 5), scores spread from 11 to 60 (range 49), only 4 of 20 above the pass mark of 50 (the classes 50-59 and 60-69 hold 4 learners). Two polygons hardly overlap (only at the class 60-69). The graphs show the difference is between subjects, as the same 20 learners are in both.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask each group to present for 1 minute. Prompt with: 'Point to the evidence on your graph for what you are claiming.' After each report ask: 'Who can add to this, or disagree?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 5 learners overall to restate another group's claim in their own words. Challenge: 'A learner says: Mrs. Wanjiku taught badly because Subject 2 is low. Does the graph prove this?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Guide: 'The graph shows what happened, not why. The test difficulty, teaching method and revision time are unknown. We call these hypotheses to investigate.' Ask: 'Which is easier to compare the two subjects, the histogram or the polygon, and why?' (the polygon puts both on one pair of axes). Link back: 'How did the graphs show patterns that the raw lists of 20 scores hid?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Whole-Class Discussion: groups state a claim, point to evidence on the graph and give reasoning. Separating what the data show from what we only suspect builds scientific reasoning and honest interpretation of data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for: correct modal classes 80-89 and 30-39; use of the words 'spread' or 'cluster' with reference to the graph; a claim that compares both subjects; statements like 'the graph cannot tell us why'. Red flags: claiming the cause of the low scores; saying the learners are 'weak' in general (the same learners are in both subjects); confusing frequency with score. Use a 3-point rubric (claim, evidence from the graph, appropriate caution) on each group's manila paper.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board: 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' They add to the board (on sticky notes) (1) what the graphs helped answer, such as 'Subject 2 needs help for the learners below 50' and (2) new questions, for example 'How can we tell the pass rate from a graph?', 'What would a second test look like on the same graph?', 'How do we find the median and quartiles from a graph?' Learners sort the sticky notes into 'Answered by Lesson 6', 'Still to find out' and 'Need more data'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which of our questions can the histograms and polygons help to answer now?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to place a note and explain why. Ask: 'What new question has the picture made you ask?' Take 3 volunteers and 2 cold-calls. Point out that the question about medians and quartiles from a graph leads to the next lesson (cumulative frequency and ogives). Ask: 'What data would we need to find out why Subject 2 is lower?' to reinforce that causes need more data (for example topic-by-topic marks, a second test).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with Question Sorting: sorting learner questions links new evidence to the driving question, shows what is answered and what is not, and gives learners ownership of the next steps of the investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 8 notes show a link between the graphs and the driving question; look for questions about reading shape or spread, cumulative totals or further data. Note learners who still ask only 'why did they score low?' without suggesting data to collect. Record the sorted categories on the board for Lesson 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update the class model for the driving question in their exercise books or on a large chart. The model so far includes: ordered lists and pass/fail counts, grouped table, mean/median/mode. They add a new section 'Pictures of the data': a sketch of both histograms or the two polygons on the same axes, with labels 'Subject 1: high, tightly clustered, modal class 80-89' and 'Subject 2: low, widely spread, modal class 30-39'. They write 2 sentences: 'The graphs show that ___. This suggests the next step is ___, but we need more data to find ___.' Exit ticket: 'Why must the two polygons use the same axes scales?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add today's evidence to our model. What does the picture show that the table alone did not?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to read their sentences. Prompt: 'Which next step for Mr. Otieno's class and which for Mrs. Wanjiku's class does the graph support?' Expected: Subject 1 learners continue with extension or enrichment work; for Subject 2, reteach and run remedial support for learners below 50. Add: 'Why do we still need a second test or topic marks?' Collect exit tickets and check them. Assign homework: draw the frequency polygon for the daily mandazi sales in Mombasa (a short grouped table given on the board) to practise boundaries and midpoints; the data must not change the anchor data.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: adding graphs to the model lets learners link earlier evidence (tables, measures) with a visual representation, strengthening their understanding of how organised data supports decisions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit-ticket indicator: learners state that the same axes and scales make the comparison fair, or that unequal scales would give a misleading picture. Check the model for the correct labels (modal classes 80-89 and 30-39), a sentence about spread, and an appropriate statement about needing more data. Record learners needing support to redraw boundaries or midpoints for a short intervention before Lesson 7.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners could draw bars at the boundaries (9.5 to 99.5) and plot the polygon at midpoints (14.5 to 94.5) without help, and which still used class limits or left gaps? Did learners distinguish what the graphs show (shape, spread, modal class) from why the scores differ? How did the same-axes comparison change learners' predictions? What support do I need to give before Lesson 7 so that learners can use their graph skills to build the cumulative frequency table and ogive?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We drew histograms (bars touching at the boundaries 9.5 to 99.5) and frequency polygons (points at midpoints 14.5 to 94.5, closed to the axis) for Subject 1 and Subject 2 on the same axes. Subject 1: scores clustered between 60 and 99, tallest bar 80-89 (f = 8). Subject 2: scores spread from 10 to 69, tallest bar 30-39 (f = 5).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A histogram shows the frequency of each class with bars at the class boundaries; a frequency polygon joins (midpoint, frequency) points and is closed at the empty classes either side. Using the same classes and scales for both subjects makes the comparison fair, and the graphs make shape and spread easy to see.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The graphs show that Subject 1 is high and tightly clustered while Subject 2 is low and widely spread, so the difference is between subjects and not about the learners all being weak. The graphs cannot tell us why the scores differ, so we need more data (for example topic-by-topic marks and a second test) before concluding.

LESSONS.title: Representation of Data II: Cumulative Frequency and Ogives
LESSONS.aresKeywords: cumulative frequency, ogive, upper class boundary, median, lower quartile, upper quartile, interquartile range, estimate, spread

slo.purpose: To build a cumulative frequency table for each subject, draw an ogive, and read off the median, quartiles and interquartile range as estimates, so that the class can use position and spread to predict next steps for the learners and for Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku.
slo.knowledge: Learners will: (1) build a cumulative frequency (less-than) table using the upper class boundaries 59.5 to 99.5 for Subject 1 and 9.5 to 69.5 for Subject 2, and check that the last cf equals n = 20; (2) draw an ogive by plotting (upper boundary, cf) points; (3) read the median (10th value), Q1 (5th value) and Q3 (15th value) from the ogive as estimates; (4) calculate the estimated IQR = Q3 - Q1 (Subject 1: 13.2; Subject 2: 24.2); (5) check the ogive median against the grouped median formula from Lesson 5 (80.75 and 33.5).
slo.skills: Developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2): turning a table into a graph and using the graph to find values. Analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4): reading quartiles from the ogive and comparing spread. Using mathematics and computational thinking (SEP 5): calculating cf, positions n/4, n/2, 3n/4 and the IQR. Constructing explanations (SEP 6): using the ogive to justify a statement about the two subjects. Communication: groups of 4 present ogives on manila paper.
slo.attitudes: Learners will show patience and accuracy when plotting and reading graphs, respect for the evidence in the data when it differs from first impressions, and teamwork when sharing graph-drawing roles. They will be cautious about claiming reasons for the scores, using words like 'may' and 'we need more data'.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? 2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 6 showed the raw and ordered scores, the frequency tables, the measures and the histograms and polygons. Lesson 7 adds a new tool, the ogive. It lets the class read the median and quartiles directly and measure spread with the IQR (13.2 for Subject 1, 24.2 for Subject 2). This supplies the evidence for Lesson 8, where all the summaries are used together to compare the subjects and predict next steps.
slo.safetyNotes: Use sharp pencils and rulers carefully. Keep walkways clear when groups display manila paper. Learners share rulers and graph paper so that no one is excluded. Stay in seats while measuring on the large class graph.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng has asked the Grade 10 class at the day secondary school in Kisumu to use the data from Mr. Otieno's Subject 1 and Mrs. Wanjiku's Subject 2 to decide next steps. Learners have ordered the scores, tabulated them, calculated measures and drawn histograms and polygons. In this lesson they ask a new question: 'If we line up all 20 learners from lowest to highest, what score marks the halfway learner, the learner a quarter of the way up, and the learner three quarters of the way up?' They build cumulative frequency tables (for example, Subject 2: 13 learners scored below 39.5), plot ogives on the same axes, and read the median, Q1 and Q3 as estimates. They compare the readings with the grouped median formula from Lesson 5 and discuss why the ogive shows spread (IQR 13.2 against 24.2). Learners treat any reasons for the difference as hypotheses and avoid claiming causes.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the Subject 2 grouped frequency table from Lesson 3 and Madam Achieng's question: 'How many learners scored less than 40 in Subject 2?' They first predict individually and then in pairs. They write: (a) their estimate of the number of learners below 39.5 and (b) which score they think the middle learner (the 10th) has in each subject. Then they sketch what they think a graph of 'number of learners below each score' would look like for Subject 1 and for Subject 2, marking whether it climbs early or late. Common predictions might be: Subject 2 climbs early and Subject 1 climbs late, because Subject 1 has no scores below 67. Learners record the predictions in their books and on a class chart to revisit in the Explain Phase.
framework.teacherMoves: Write on the board: 'Mr. Otieno's class scored 67 to 95. Mrs. Wanjiku's class scored 11 to 60. Madam Achieng asks: how many learners are below 40 in Subject 2?' Say: 'Do not calculate yet. Use the table from Lesson 3 and make your best prediction.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds in silence. Then ask: 'Turn to your partner: where on the number line is the middle learner in Subject 2, and why do you think so?' Cold-call 4 pairs, including at least 2 who have not spoken in the last lesson. Ask: 'What would a graph that counts learners up to each score look like?' Accept sketches and say: 'We will test your sketches with evidence.' Do not correct predictions yet. Record them on a chart headed 'Our Predictions'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with sketch-and-justify: learners commit to a prediction and a rough sketch before instruction, so their ideas become visible. Revisiting them later lets learners see how evidence changes their thinking, and it gives the teacher a baseline for misconceptions, such as confusing frequency with cumulative frequency.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who write a number between 0 and 20 for learners below 40 (a sensible range) versus those who write the frequency of one class only; (2) sketches that rise from left to right (a sign of understanding 'running total'), versus sketches that look like histograms; (3) justifications that refer to the table, such as 'Subject 2 has many scores in the 10s to 30s'. Note on a class list which learners show the histogram misconception so that you can support them in the Observe Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (cumulative frequency tables, about 20 minutes): In groups of 4 learners start with the grouped table from Lesson 3 (Subject 1: 60-69: 2, 70-79: 7, 80-89: 8, 90-99: 3; Subject 2: 10-19: 4, 20-29: 4, 30-39: 5, 40-49: 3, 50-59: 2, 60-69: 2). They write the upper class boundaries and build less-than cumulative frequency (cf) columns. Subject 1: <59.5: 0; <69.5: 2; <79.5: 9; <89.5: 17; <99.5: 20. Subject 2: <9.5: 0; <19.5: 4; <29.5: 8; <39.5: 13; <49.5: 16; <59.5: 18; <69.5: 20. They check that the last cf is 20 and compare with the ordered lists. For example, in Subject 2 the scores below 39.5 are 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 23, 27, 29, 30, 31, 32, 32, 35, which is 13. Part B (drawing ogives, about 35 minutes): Each group draws two ogives on the same axes, with score on the horizontal axis (0 to 100) and cf on the vertical axis (0 to 20). Each ogive starts at the lower boundary of the first class with cf 0 (Subject 1 at 59.5; Subject 2 at 9.5) and uses points (upper boundary, cf), joined with a smooth curve. Roles: reader of values, plotter, ruler holder, checker. Part C (reading the ogive, about 15 minutes): learners draw lines at cf = 5, 10 and 15 (n/4, n/2, 3n/4), read the scores and record: Subject 1 Q1 about 73.8, median about 80.75, Q3 about 87.0; Subject 2 Q1 22.0, median 33.5, Q3 about 46.2. They calculate the IQRs: 13.2 and 24.2. Learners write that all are estimates because the data is grouped.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one row on the board: 'The class 30-39 has f = 5. The cf up to 39.5 is 4 + 4 + 5 = 13. What does the 13 tell us about learners?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to say in words: '13 learners scored less than 39.5 in Subject 2.' Circulate while groups build tables and ask: 'Which boundary do we plot against, the lower, the upper or the midpoint? Why?' If a group uses midpoints, say: 'That is what we did for the polygon in Lesson 6. Here the cf counts everyone up to the END of the class, so what value does the end of the class have?' Prompt: 'Why does Subject 1 start at 59.5 with cf 0?' During drawing say: 'Use the same scales on both ogives so we can compare fairly.' Check axes, scales and the first point. During reading ask: 'Where is the 10th learner on your graph? Draw across from 10, then down. What score do you read?' Remind learners to write 'about' or 'estimate'. Stop after 10 minutes and ask 3 groups to share their Subject 2 median reading with the class, writing the values on the board (accept 33 to 34).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-to-graph modelling with structured roles: learners convert a table into a visual model and then extract information from the model. Roles ensure that everyone handles the data, and reading across and down from the cf axis makes the idea of 'the halfway learner' concrete. Using the same axes for both subjects supports comparison, as in the histograms of Lesson 6.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) cf columns that increase and end at 20; (2) points plotted at upper boundaries (e.g. (39.5, 13)), not midpoints; (3) ogives that start at 59.5 and 9.5 with cf 0 and never go down; (4) reading lines drawn across at 5, 10 and 15 and then down to the score axis; (5) estimates within about 1 mark of the values: Subject 1 Q1 73.8, median 80.75, Q3 87.0; Subject 2 Q1 22.0, median 33.5, Q3 46.2; (6) learners use the word 'estimate'. Use a checklist as you circulate and mark groups that need help with boundaries or scales.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners meet in their groups and compare their ogive readings with the grouped median formula from Lesson 5. They calculate Subject 1: median = 79.5 + ((10 - 9)/8) x 10 = 80.75, and Subject 2: median = 29.5 + ((10 - 8)/5) x 10 = 33.5. They compare these with their ogive readings and compare both with the exact ungrouped medians (80.5 and 31.5), noting that grouped values are estimates and differ slightly. They also verify Q1 for Subject 2 by interpolation: 19.5 + (1/4)(10) = 22.0 and Q3: 39.5 + (2/3)(10) = 46.2. Next they explain the shapes of the two ogives: Subject 2 rises steeply on the left (many low scores) and flattens as the scores stop at 69.5; Subject 1 stays flat at 0 until 59.5, then rises steeply between 69.5 and 89.5. Then they compare IQRs (13.2 and 24.2) and complete a sentence frame: 'The middle half of Subject 1 scores lies between __ and __, a width of __, while the middle half of Subject 2 lies between __ and __, a width of __. This shows that __.' They also discuss: 'Did your prediction about the climb of the graphs match?' Finally they discuss what the ogive does not tell us: it does not show why the scores differ, and reasons such as test difficulty, teaching method or revision time are hypotheses that need more data.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Your ogive says the Subject 2 median is about 33.5. The formula in Lesson 5 gave 33.5. Why would these agree?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Follow up: 'The exact median from the ordered list was 31.5. Why is 33.5 not the same?' Elicit that grouped data hides the exact scores inside each class. Ask: 'Which subject has the larger IQR? What does a larger IQR tell Madam Achieng?' Cold-call 4 learners, accepting 'the middle half of learners are more spread out in Subject 2'. Challenge: 'A learner says Mrs. Wanjiku must be a weaker teacher because the scores are lower. Does the ogive prove that?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Guide: 'The data shows WHAT happened, not WHY. Rewrite the claim using the words may or could.' Have 2 groups read their revised statements aloud. Return to the Predict Phase chart and ask: 'Which predictions were supported? Which should we change?' Use a different colour to mark revisions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with cross-checking: learners support statements about median and spread with two methods (ogive and formula) and the graph shape. Agreement between methods builds confidence in the model, and the 'data shows what, not why' discussion trains learners to separate evidence from hypotheses. Revisiting predictions makes learning visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) learners show the working for 79.5 + (1/8)(10) = 80.75 and 29.5 + (2/5)(10) = 33.5 correctly; (2) learners say the ogive and formula values are close because both are estimates from grouped data; (3) sentence frames completed with values from 73.8 to 87.0 (width 13.2) and 22.0 to 46.2 (width 24.2); (4) statements that avoid causal claims, e.g. 'the lower scores in Subject 2 could be due to many factors, we need more data'; (5) learners explain a steep section of an ogive as 'many learners in that class'. Collect one sentence from each learner as an exit ticket.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board headed: 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' Individually they write on sticky notes (a) one thing the ogive helped them to answer, for example 'Half of the learners in Subject 2 scored below about 33.5' and (b) one new question, for example 'Why is the spread of Subject 2 larger?', 'Will a second test give the same ogive?' or 'Which topics did the 16 learners below 50 find hardest?' They place notes under the headings 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'New questions'. As a class they link new notes to earlier notes about tables, measures and graphs and decide which will be addressed next in Lesson 8, where all the summaries will be compared.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take two minutes of silent thinking. What did the ogive show that the histogram and the raw list did not?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before they write. Cold-call 4 learners to read their notes and ask the class: 'Does this answer the DQB, partly answer it, or raise a new question?' Move notes physically. Prompt: 'Which question needs more data, such as topic-by-topic marks or a second test?' Highlight that Madam Achieng's decision needs justified predictions. Link back: 'Key inquiry 1: how do we organise data? We now have tables, measures and three graphs. Key inquiry 2: why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data? Give one example from today.' Ask 2 learners to answer.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with sorting and linking: learners categorise questions as answered, partly answered or new. This shows progress, builds a record of learning and motivates the next lesson, helping learners see that understanding grows from evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) notes referring to specific values (median 33.5, IQR 24.2); (2) new questions that ask for causes or more data rather than only recalling facts; (3) correct sorting of at least one note into 'Answered' with evidence; (4) learners connect their note to a previous lesson (e.g. 'the histogram showed the shape but not the middle half'). Record which learners wrote only recall questions and prompt them with 'What would you need to find out to be sure?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update their group model (a one-page summary on manila paper) of the question 'How can the two sets of data predict next steps?'. They add a new section called 'Position and spread' that contains: both cumulative frequency tables; a short description of each ogive (Subject 1: flat until 59.5, steep from 69.5 to 89.5; Subject 2: steep early, flattening at about 59.5 to 69.5); the estimated quartiles (Subject 1: Q1 73.8, median 80.75, Q3 87.0; Subject 2: Q1 22.0, median 33.5, Q3 46.2) and IQRs (13.2 and 24.2). They add two provisional predictions, for example: 'If the pattern holds, Mr. Otieno's class may be ready for extension work' and 'Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners may need to reteach and revise Subject 2 topics and give support to the 16 learners below 50, and collect more data to find the cause.' They label predictions as provisional. Groups swap models and give one 'two stars and a wish' comment. Finally, they complete the summary table prompt in their notebooks.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add today's evidence to your model. Every prediction must point to a number from a table or graph.' Circulate and ask: 'Which value supports this prediction? What would make you change it?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to read one prediction and its supporting evidence. Challenge any prediction that claims a cause: 'How do you know it is the teaching? What else could it be?' Ask learners to rewrite using 'may' or 'could'. Close by saying: 'Next lesson we put everything together: averages, spread, shape and pass rate to compare the two subjects.' Leave models on display.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with peer feedback: learners integrate new evidence (ogive, quartiles, IQR) into an existing model and justify predictions with data. Peer feedback exposes gaps and tentative language keeps conclusions honest.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: (1) the model includes both cf tables, both ogives, and the correct quartile and IQR estimates; (2) each prediction cites a number (e.g. 'only 4 of 20 pass', 'IQR 24.2 versus 13.2'); (3) learners use tentative language and mention more data; (4) peer feedback that names specific strengths and missing evidence. Use a 3-level rubric (beginning, developing, secure) and note groups that need help with interpreting spread.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners plot at upper boundaries and start the ogives at 59.5 and 9.5 with cf 0, or did some use midpoints as in the polygon? (2) Could learners explain what 'the 10th learner' means on the cf axis? (3) Did the ogive and formula medians (80.75 and 33.5) agree in learners' work, and did they understand why they differ from the exact 80.5 and 31.5? (4) Did learners use 'may', 'could' and 'we need more data' when discussing the score difference, rather than blaming learners or teachers? (5) Which learners need more practice with scales and reading across and down? Plan a short warm-up for Lesson 8 using one quartile reading.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the cumulative frequency of Subject 2 reaches 13 by 39.5 and 20 by 69.5, while Subject 1 stays at 0 until 59.5 and then rises to 20 by 99.5. Both ogives were drawn using (upper boundary, cf) points. From the ogives we read estimates: Subject 1 Q1 73.8, median 80.75, Q3 87.0; Subject 2 Q1 22.0, median 33.5, Q3 46.2.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a cumulative frequency table adds up the frequencies to show how many learners scored below each upper boundary, and that an ogive lets us read the median (10th), Q1 (5th) and Q3 (15th) as estimates. The IQR = Q3 - Q1 is 13.2 for Subject 1 and 24.2 for Subject 2, so the middle half of Subject 2 scores is more spread out.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The ogives help us to answer the driving question by showing position and spread: Subject 1 scores are high and close together, while Subject 2 scores are lower and more spread out, with a median estimate of 33.5. This supports predictions that Mr. Otieno's class may continue with extension work and that Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners may reteach and revise, give support to the learners below 50 and collect more data. The graphs show what happened but not why, so we need more data such as topic-by-topic marks and a second test before concluding.

LESSONS.title: Interpretation of Data: Comparing Subjects and Predicting Next Steps
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one double lesson of 80 minutes if the Model Building Phase is extended)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: interpretation, compare, average, spread, shape, pass rate, prediction, evidence, estimate, quartiles, interquartile range

slo.purpose: Learners interpret tables, measures and graphs together to compare Subject 1 and Subject 2 (average, spread, shape, pass rate) and use the evidence to draw justified conclusions and predictions about the next steps for the learners, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku.
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) compare two sets of data using the mean, median, range and interquartile range (Subject 1: mean 80.35, median 80.5, range 28; Subject 2: mean 33.85, median 31.5, range 49); (2) read the shape and spread of the two histograms/frequency polygons and the two ogives; (3) use pass counts (20 of 20 in Subject 1; 4 of 20 in Subject 2, 16 below 50, and 7 learners at 40 or above) to describe performance; (4) distinguish between what the data shows and what it cannot show (the causes).
slo.skills: Analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP 4); Using mathematics and computational thinking (SEP 5); Engaging in argument from evidence (SEP 7); Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (SEP 8). Learners also practise critical thinking, communication and collaboration in groups of 4.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that data can be used fairly to make decisions per subject rather than labelling learners as 'weak' or 'clever'; they show curiosity, honesty and respect for others' views when discussing results about their own class and teachers; they accept that predictions should be revised when new data arrives.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? 2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1-7 the class ordered the scores, built frequency tables, calculated the measures and drew histograms, polygons and ogives. Lesson 8 brings all this evidence together. For the first time learners use it as one body of evidence to answer the driving question: How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps? It prepares Lesson 9, where learners write final evidence-based recommendations and revise the final model.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Handle scissors (if used to cut summary cards) carefully. Be sensitive: the scores are of one class in a day secondary school in Kisumu, so ensure no learner is blamed or laughed at. Remind learners that the data shows differences between subjects, not who is 'weak' or whose teaching is 'bad'. Keep groupwork spaces clear of bags and desks to avoid tripping.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng, the Deputy Principal of a day secondary school in Kisumu, has asked the Grade 10 class to use the data to decide next steps. The same 20 learners scored 67 to 95 in Subject 1 (Mr. Otieno) and only 11 to 60 in Subject 2 (Mrs. Wanjiku). In this lesson learners put together everything gathered so far: tables, measures (mean 80.35 vs 33.85; median 80.5 vs 31.5; range 28 vs 49; IQR 13.5 vs 22.5), graphs (histograms, polygons, ogives) and pass counts (20 vs 4). In groups of 4 they build a comparison on manila paper, practise writing claim-evidence-reasoning statements, and predict next steps while separating what the data shows from what it cannot explain (causes remain hypotheses). The lesson answers Key Inquiry 2 by showing how organised data reveals patterns that the raw lists hid.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look again at the two raw lists on the board (Subject 1: 72, 85, 90, 67, 78 ... ; Subject 2: 35, 42, 27, 58, 44 ...). Individually they write on a sticky note or in their exercise book: 'If I were Madam Achieng, the one thing I would do next for Subject 1 is ___, and for Subject 2 is ___, because ___.' Then they predict which summary measures (mean, median, range, IQR, pass count) and which graph will give the strongest evidence for their decision. They share with a partner (Think-Pair-Share) and keep their predictions for later checking.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the two raw lists and say: 'Last week you turned these lists into tables and graphs. Madam Achieng now wants a decision. Before we look at our summaries, write your first prediction.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question, silently counting. Ask: 'Which would help you more to decide, the raw list or the histogram? Why?' Cold-call 4 learners from different groups, including at least 2 who have not spoken yet, and record predictions on the board under two headings: 'Learners' and 'Teachers'. Say: 'Keep your prediction. We will test it against the evidence today.' Do not correct predictions; ask 'What evidence would change your mind?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with Think-Pair-Share: Writing a prediction first surfaces learners' prior ideas (such as 'Subject 2 learners are weak') and makes them accountable to evidence. Pair talk lets learners rehearse reasoning before the class discussion, so the later comparison with the data is a real test of their thinking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) predictions that mention at least one measure or graph (e.g. 'the mean', 'the pass count') rather than only opinions; (b) whether learners predict a different action for each subject; (c) whether any learners blame learners' ability or the teachers without evidence. Tally these on a class list. Learners who write only opinions are prompted with 'Which number would show that?'

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners receive a Data Summary Pack (prepared from Lessons 4-7) with: both ascending lists, the grouped frequency table, the two histograms/frequency polygons on the same axes, the two ogives on the same axes, and a blank comparison table. They fill in the table: Mean (80.35 / 33.85), Median (80.5 / 31.5), Mode (none / 32 and 60), Range (28 / 49), Q1 and Q3 (73.5, 87 / 22, 44.5), IQR (13.5 / 22.5), lowest and highest score (67 and 95 / 11 and 60), pass count (20 / 4), fail count (0 / 16), and learners at 40 or more (20 / 7). They then annotate the graphs: where the tallest bar is (80-89 for Subject 1; 30-39 for Subject 2), where the polygons overlap (only the 60-69 class, with 2 learners each), and where each ogive rises steepest. They note that grouped estimates (mean 80.5 and 35; median 80.75 and 33.5) differ slightly from the exact values. Each group records three observations in the form 'I notice ___ in the ___ (table/graph/measure).'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your job now is to be data detectives. Look only at what the numbers and graphs show. Do not say why yet.' Circulate to every group. Ask: 'Where on the histogram can you see that all 20 learners passed Subject 1?' (WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds.) Ask: 'Which class in Subject 2 has the most learners, and how many?' Ask: 'Subject 2 has a bigger range, 49 compared with 28. What does that look like on the graph?' Prompt groups that rely on a single measure: 'The means are 80.35 and 33.85. Does the mean alone show the spread? What else tells you?' Remind: 'Grouped values are estimates, so they differ slightly from exact ones.' Cold-call 3 groups to report one observation each, and write them on the board in a 'We observe' column. Check the first group's pass count of 4 (51, 58, 60, 60) against the ascending list.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Discourse / Noticing and Wondering with multiple representations: Learners connect the same fact across a table, a measure and a graph (for example, 'range 49' and 'wide polygon'). Seeing one idea in three forms builds a more robust understanding and helps them see why raw lists hid patterns.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that the comparison table is correctly completed (means 80.35 and 33.85, medians 80.5 and 31.5, ranges 28 and 49, IQRs 13.5 and 22.5, pass counts 20 and 4). Look for learners who correctly point to the 80-89 and 30-39 classes on the graphs, correctly describe the narrow cluster against the wide spread, and use the word 'estimate' for grouped values. Note any learner who confuses the range with the IQR or the pass count with the number of learners at 40 or above (7), and address it on the spot.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group writes three Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statements on manila paper. Example Claim: 'Subject 1 scores are higher and more tightly clustered than Subject 2 scores.' Evidence: 'mean 80.35 vs 33.85; median 80.5 vs 31.5; range 28 vs 49; IQR 13.5 vs 22.5.' Reasoning: 'A higher average with a smaller range means most learners in Subject 1 scored close to the top, while in Subject 2 scores are low and far apart.' Other required claims: (2) 'All 20 learners passed Subject 1 but only 4 passed Subject 2, so the same learners cannot all be weak; the difference is between subjects.' (3) 'In Subject 2, 7 learners scored 40 or more, and 16 are below the pass mark of 50, so some learners need remedial support.' Groups then write predicted next steps: for learners, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku. They also write one 'We cannot yet say' statement, for example 'We cannot say why Subject 2 scores were low; the test may have been harder, the topics may not have been revised, or the teaching method may differ. We need more data.' Groups display their work in a gallery walk, and each learner adds one star and one question to another group's paper.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one CER on the board with Subject 1 and say: 'A good claim is checked by numbers. Which number proves it? How does the number prove it?' Insist: 'Use the words may, could, we need more data when you talk about reasons.' Ask: 'Mrs. Wanjiku's class has a lower mean. Does that prove she is a poor teacher?' (WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds.) Guide learners to see that the data cannot tell us. Ask: 'Could the test have been harder? What data would show that?' (Topic-by-topic marks, a second test.) Cold-call 5 learners during the gallery walk to explain another group's claim in their own words. Challenge outliers: 'Subject 1's highest score is 95, Subject 2's is 60. Does a high maximum mean the subject is easier? What else do we check?' Use Kenyan comparisons if needed: 'If one farmer in Kericho picks tea quickly and another is slower, can we say why from the kilograms alone?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (argument from evidence) with a Gallery Walk: CER forces learners to connect each claim to specific numbers and to explain how the numbers support the claim. Distinguishing 'what the data shows' from 'what we cannot yet say' builds scientific and statistical honesty. The gallery walk exposes learners to alternative reasoning and prompts peer critique.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a checklist for each group: Does each claim cite at least two numbers? Is the reasoning linked to spread and average, not only to the average? Does the group avoid claiming causes as facts? Do they state 16 below 50 and 7 at 40 or above correctly? Successful indicators: learners use 'may' or 'could' when giving reasons. If a group writes 'Mrs. Wanjiku teaches badly', ask them to rewrite the statement as a hypothesis that could be tested.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the question 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' They move sticky notes: questions answered by the evidence (for example 'Did the same learners pass both subjects?' - answered: all 20 passed Subject 1, 4 passed Subject 2) go to an 'Answered' column with a short evidence note. New questions are added, such as 'Was the Subject 2 test harder than the Subject 1 test?', 'Which Subject 2 topics lost the most marks?', 'Will a second test show the same pattern?', 'Would the same pattern appear in other classes?' Each learner writes at least one new question and one answer with evidence, referring to the Kisumu class data.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the DQB. Which of our questions can we now answer with numbers? Which cannot be answered with the data we have?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to move a question to 'Answered' and justify it with a number. Ask: 'What new question has today's comparison raised?' Highlight questions about causes and say: 'Those are questions for more data. In Lesson 9 we will decide which data to collect and write our recommendations.' Ensure that each group adds at least one question. Point out the link to Key Inquiry 2: 'Which question on the board shows why collecting and interpreting data matters?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question sorting: Sorting questions into 'answered by evidence' and 'needs more data' makes progress visible and turns gaps in the evidence into purposeful next investigations. It keeps the learners' own questions at the centre of the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners can support 'Answered' with a specific piece of evidence (such as pass count 20 vs 4, or range 28 vs 49). Check that new questions are testable (for example, 'topic-by-topic marks' rather than 'Is Mrs. Wanjiku good?'). Note learners who add questions about causes and praise them as good scientific thinking.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their class model, a flow diagram on manila paper titled 'From Raw Scores to Decisions': Raw lists -> Ascending order -> Frequency tables -> Mean, median, mode, range, quartiles -> Histograms, polygons and ogives -> Comparison and interpretation -> Predictions and next steps. In this lesson they add the Interpretation stage with the boxes: 'Compare average (80.35 vs 33.85)', 'Compare spread (range 28 vs 49, IQR 13.5 vs 22.5)', 'Compare pass rate (20 vs 4)', and 'What we cannot say yet: causes'. They then draft predictions: Mr. Otieno's class: continue and give extension or enrichment work; Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners: reteach and revise the Subject 2 topics, remedial support for the 16 learners below 50, and collect more data (topic-by-topic marks, a second test). Learners also compare these with their original predictions from the Predict Phase and write one sentence: 'My first prediction changed/stayed the same because ___.' Finally, each learner completes an exit ticket: 'Using one table, one measure and one graph, explain why Madam Achieng should make a separate decision for each subject.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model should now show how the data led you to a decision. Where does today's work fit?' Ask groups to point to the arrow where interpretation happens. Ask: 'If the Subject 2 mean rises to 50 in the second test, which parts of your model would change?' (WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds.) Cold-call 3 groups to read their predictions and justify each with one number. Press: 'Is this a prediction or a fact? What word shows that?' Check that learners say 'estimate' for grouped measures. Collect exit tickets. Tell the class: 'In Lesson 9 we write the final recommendations for Madam Achieng and revise this model for the last time.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Prediction Reflection: Adding the interpretation stage to the evolving model shows how each lesson's skill (ordering, tabulating, summarising, graphing) contributes to decisions. Comparing the new predictions with the Predict Phase ideas develops metacognition and shows that evidence can change thinking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that the revised model includes the interpretation stage and the 'cannot say yet' box. In the exit ticket, look for: a correct number from a table (such as the pass count 20 vs 4), a correct measure (such as the mean 80.35 vs 33.85 or range 28 vs 49), a reference to a graph (histogram, polygon or ogive), and a conclusion for each subject. Proficient responses state that decisions should be made per subject and that more data is needed to find causes.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Which groups used both an average and a spread measure in their claims, and which relied only on the mean? (2) Did any learners write causes as facts (for example 'Mrs. Wanjiku is not teaching well')? How did I respond, and how can I reinforce the idea of hypotheses in Lesson 9? (3) Could learners read the ogives and histograms accurately and distinguish the exact values (80.35, 33.85) from the grouped estimates (80.5, 35)? (4) Did learners confuse the 16 learners below 50 with the 7 learners at 40 or above? (5) Were cold-calls distributed fairly, and did every learner speak at least once? (6) Which DQB questions need to be addressed in Lesson 9, and what extra data (topic-by-topic marks, a second test) will the class suggest? Record two changes to make next time.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that Subject 1 scores are high and tightly clustered (mean 80.35, median 80.5, range 28, all 20 learners pass) while Subject 2 scores are low and widely spread (mean 33.85, median 31.5, range 49, only 4 of 20 pass, 16 below 50, 7 at 40 or more). The histograms, polygons and ogives show the same pattern: the Subject 1 graphs are narrow and to the right, and the Subject 2 graphs are wide and to the left.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that tables, measures and graphs must be read together to compare two sets of data using average, spread, shape and pass rate. We learned that the grouped values are estimates, and that the data shows differences between subjects but cannot tell us why the scores differ.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explain that the same 20 learners cannot all be weak, because they all passed Subject 1 but most failed Subject 2, so decisions must be made per subject. We predict that Mr. Otieno's class should continue with extension or enrichment work, and that Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners should reteach and revise the Subject 2 topics, give remedial support to the 16 learners below 50, and collect more data (such as topic-by-topic marks and a second test) before concluding why the scores differ.
