LESSONS.title: Why Collecting, Organising and Interpreting Data Leads to Effective Decisions
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (1 double lesson of 80 minutes if available; core activities fit in 40 minutes)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: data, frequency distribution table, mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range, histogram, frequency polygon, ogive, recommendation, evidence, decision

slo.purpose: To bring together everything learned in Lessons 1-8 to write evidence-based recommendations that answer the driving question, and to show why collecting, organising and interpreting data supports effective decisions.
slo.knowledge: Learners will explain, using the Key Comparison, that Subject 1 scores are high and tightly clustered (mean 80.35, median 80.5, range 28, all 20 pass) while Subject 2 scores are low and widely spread (mean 33.85, median 31.5, range 49, 4 of 20 pass), and that organised data shows patterns that the raw lists hid.
slo.skills: Learners will interpret tables, measures and graphs together; justify recommendations using numerical evidence; separate what the data shows from what it cannot show (causes); compare their Lesson 1 model with the final model; and communicate conclusions on manila paper (NGSS SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence; Developing and Using Models; Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information).
slo.attitudes: Learners will value evidence over opinion, show fairness to learners and teachers by not blaming without data, and collaborate respectfully in groups of 4.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables? 2. Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson. In Lesson 1 learners only had raw and ordered lists and could say who passed or failed. Lessons 2-3 organised the data into frequency tables, Lessons 4-5 summarised it with mean, median and mode, Lessons 6-7 graphed it (histograms, polygons, ogives, quartiles) and Lesson 8 compared the subjects. Lesson 9 turns that evidence into the final explanation and recommendations that answer the driving question: How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Remind learners to handle manila paper and markers sensibly, keep walkways clear during the gallery walk, and speak respectfully about learners and teachers: we discuss data, not people. Be sensitive to learners who may personally relate to low scores; frame results as information about the subject test, not about any learner's ability.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng, the Deputy Principal of the day secondary school in Kisumu, has asked the Grade 10 class for a final report on the two sets of scores of the same 20 learners. Learners revisit the Driving Question Board, collect the evidence gathered across Lessons 1-8, and use it to write recommendations for Mr. Otieno (Subject 1), Mrs. Wanjiku (Subject 2), the learners, and the 16 learners below 50 in Subject 2. They compare their Lesson 1 model (raw and ordered lists, pass/fail only) with a final model (tables, measures, graphs and interpretation), complete the DQB, and write a Final Explanation of why collecting, organising and interpreting data leads to effective decisions. Throughout, reasons for the score difference are treated as hypotheses to investigate (test difficulty, teaching method, revision time are unknown), not facts.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the phenomenon: the same 20 learners scored 67 to 95 in Subject 1 and 11 to 60 in Subject 2. Individually, then in pairs, they write a 2-3 sentence prediction on a sticky note or in their notebooks: 'If Madam Achieng only had the raw lists, what would she decide? If she has all our tables, measures and graphs, what will she decide, and how sure can she be?' They also predict which of these decisions are safe to make now and which need more data (for example, 'Are the learners weak?' or 'Is the Subject 2 test too hard?').
framework.teacherMoves: Display the two raw lists on the board next to a blank space. Say: 'Madam Achieng is waiting for our report. Before we write it, take two minutes silently. What would she decide from the raw lists alone? What could she decide now that we have organised the data?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds after the question before anyone speaks. Circulate and note 3 different predictions. Cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) to share, including at least one who predicted 'the learners are weak'. Record predictions on the board under the heading 'Predictions Today'. Do not correct yet; say: 'We will test these predictions against our evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction before evidence): Committing to a prediction makes learners aware of their starting ideas, so when the evidence is revisited they can see how much their thinking has changed since Lesson 1, and any misconception (for example 'learners are weak') becomes visible and testable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (a) learners who predict a single decision for all 20 learners across both subjects (misconception: learners are simply 'weak' or 'strong'); (b) learners who name at least one measure or graph they would use; (c) learners who write 'we need to know why' or similar, showing awareness that causes are unknown. Tally the three types of responses on the board to guide later questioning.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners lay out the evidence 'portfolio' they have built over Lessons 1-8: the ordered lists and pass/fail counts (Lesson 1), the frequency tables (Lessons 2-3), the means, medians and modes (Lessons 4-5), the histograms and frequency polygons (Lesson 6) and the ogives and quartiles (Lesson 7). They fill in an Evidence Summary Table on manila paper with these rows for Subject 1 and Subject 2: mean (80.35 / 33.85), median (80.5 / 31.5), mode (none / 32 and 60), range (28 / 49), IQR (13.5 / 22.5), lowest and highest score (67 and 95 / 11 and 60), number passing (20 / 4), modal class (80-89 / 30-39). They also note the 7 learners who scored 40 or more in Subject 2 and that 16 of 20 are below the pass mark of 50. Each group checks that every figure is traceable to a table or graph, and agrees on the shape of each histogram (Subject 1 clustered between 60 and 99, Subject 2 spread from 10 to 69 with most below 50).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your portfolios. Your job is to gather the evidence, not to decide yet. Every number you write in your Evidence Summary Table must have a source: which table or graph did it come from?' Circulate with a checklist; ask each group: 'Show me where the 31.5 comes from.' and 'Where on your histogram do you see the spread of 49?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds after each question before prompting. Cold-call 3 groups to read one row each of their table aloud while the class checks against the Key Comparison on the board. Where a group's figure differs (for example grouped estimate 80.5 vs exact 80.35), prompt: 'Why might these two means differ slightly?' (grouped values are estimates using midpoints). Keep the anchor numbers exactly as given; do not accept invented values.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence Table with Source Tracing (Obtaining and Evaluating Information): Requiring a source for each value builds the habit of tying claims to data, and placing both subjects side by side makes the pattern of higher and tighter versus lower and wider visible at a glance, which the raw lists hid.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: every row of the table is filled correctly with values matching the established data; learners can point to the correct table or graph for each value; learners distinguish exact values (80.35, 33.85) from grouped estimates (80.5, 35); learners state that 20 of 20 pass in Subject 1 and 4 of 20 pass in Subject 2. Note groups that mix up mean and median or misread the IQR for targeted support.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups write evidence-based recommendations for four audiences using a 'Claim-Evidence-Reasoning-Limit' frame: (1) Mr. Otieno and the Subject 1 class: continue and give extension or enrichment work, because all 20 learners passed with scores tightly clustered (mean 80.35, median 80.5, range 28); (2) Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners: reteach and revise the Subject 2 topics, because the mean is 33.85, the median is 31.5 and only 4 of 20 passed; (3) the 16 learners below 50 in Subject 2: remedial support, with the 7 learners at 40 or above as those closest to the pass mark; (4) Madam Achieng: collect more data, such as topic-by-topic marks and a second test, before concluding why Subject 2 scores are low. For each recommendation, learners write the Claim, the numerical Evidence, the Reasoning (why this evidence supports the claim) and a Limit (what the data cannot tell us, for example 'we do not know if the Subject 2 test was harder, how it was taught, or how long learners revised'). They also write one sentence answering: 'Can the same learners all be weak?' (No: the same 20 learners did well in Subject 1, so the difference is between subjects and decisions must be made per subject.)
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Madam Achieng does not want opinions. She wants recommendations she can trust. For each recommendation, give a claim, the numbers that support it, your reasoning, and one thing the data cannot tell us.' Model one example on the board for Mr. Otieno, then let groups write the other three. WAIT TIME: 15 seconds of silent thinking before group writing begins. Circulate and ask: 'Which number convinces you most? Why that one and not the mean alone?' and 'Is that a fact from the data or a hypothesis we still need to test?' Challenge any statement such as 'Mrs. Wanjiku taught badly' or 'the test was too hard' with: 'What data shows that? What data would we need?' Cold-call 4 groups (one per audience) to read their recommendations; ask 2 other groups to give a thumbs-up or thumbs-down on whether the evidence supports the claim and why. Use 'may', 'could' and 'we need more data' in your own language.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning-Limit (Engaging in Argument from Evidence): Linking each recommendation to specific numbers and to an honest limit teaches learners that effective decisions rest on organised data and that unexplained causes are hypotheses, not conclusions. Peer critique strengthens reasoning and corrects overreach.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: each recommendation cites at least two correct figures from the Key Comparison; learners include a limit that names unknown causes (test difficulty, teaching method, revision time) without asserting any as true; learners decide per subject rather than labelling learners 'weak'; learners recommend collecting more data (second test, topic-by-topic marks). Use a 3-level checklist (claim only / claim with numbers / claim, numbers and limit) and record each group's level.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board and the question: 'How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' In groups they sort the DQB questions generated across the unit (for example 'Why are the raw lists hard to read?', 'How can we show spread?', 'Which average should we trust?', 'Why did the same learners score differently?') into three columns: Answered by our data, Partly answered, Needs more data. Each group moves two question cards and justifies the move with a piece of evidence (for example 'How can we show spread?' is answered by range 28 versus 49, IQR 13.5 versus 22.5, and the histograms). Learners add at least one new question to the 'Needs more data' column (for example 'Which topics in Subject 2 did the 16 learners find hardest?', 'Will a second test give similar results?', 'Would the same pattern appear in Subject 1 if the test were harder?'). Finally, learners write a one-sentence answer to the driving question on a card and pin it at the top of the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board has grown since Lesson 1. Let us see what we can now answer.' Hold up three question cards one at a time and ask: 'Which column does this belong in, and what is your evidence?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds before taking responses. Cold-call 5 different learners to move a card and justify the move; ask a follow-up to a second learner: 'Do you agree? What evidence supports or challenges that?' Highlight that the question 'Why did the same learners score differently?' stays in 'Needs more data' because the data does not tell us the cause. Praise questions that identify new data to collect. Photograph the final DQB for the class record.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board sorting (tracking growing understanding): Moving questions between columns with evidence makes progress visible, shows learners which questions data can answer and which require further collection, and links the two KICD key inquiry questions to the class's own questions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners justify card moves with specific data (for example a measure or graph); they correctly leave the 'why' question under 'Needs more data'; they generate at least one new, testable question about data to collect; their one-sentence answer to the driving question names both subjects and a next step. Record learners who cannot justify a move for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Lesson 1 model (a sketch or short note showing the raw and ordered lists, who passed or failed, and the questions about patterns, spread and action needed). On a fresh half of manila paper they build a Final Model as a flow diagram: Collect (the 20 scores in each subject) → Organise (ascending order, frequency tables with class width 10, cumulative frequency) → Summarise (mean, median, mode, range, quartiles) → Graph (histogram, frequency polygon, ogive) → Interpret (Subject 1 high and clustered; Subject 2 low and spread out; same learners, so differences are between subjects) → Decide (recommendations per subject) → Collect more data (second test, topic-by-topic marks). Beside the model, learners complete a comparison table: 'Lesson 1 model: what we could see / could not see' versus 'Final model: what we can see now'. They then write the Final Explanation in 5-6 sentences answering the second key inquiry question: 'Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions?' using at least three numbers from the Key Comparison. Groups carry out a short gallery walk: each group leaves one member to explain while the others visit, then they swap roles and give each other one star (strong evidence) and one wish (a missing limit or number).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Place your Lesson 1 model next to your Final Model. What can you see now that you could not see then?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds of silent thinking, then 2 minutes of pair talk. Provide sentence starters on the board: 'In Lesson 1 we could only say... Now we can say... because...' and 'Organising the data helped us see... which the raw lists hid.' Circulate and press for specifics: 'Which graph shows the spread best?' and 'Where does your model show that we do not yet know the cause?' Cold-call 4 learners to read their Final Explanation sentences; invite 2 others to add or challenge a point. Close by saying: 'So, how can the two sets of data be used to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?' and take responses from 3 more learners. Collect the Final Explanations and models for assessment.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Comparison (Developing and Using Models): Placing the Lesson 1 model beside the final one lets learners see their own conceptual growth, and writing a Final Explanation requires them to connect organising, summarising, graphing and interpreting to decision-making. The gallery walk with star and wish feedback strengthens communication of evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: the Final Model includes all stages (collect, organise, summarise, graph, interpret, decide, collect more data); the comparison table identifies at least two things the raw lists hid (spread, clustering, differences between subjects, pass rate); the Final Explanation uses at least three correct values (for example 80.35, 33.85, 28, 49, 20 of 20, 4 of 20) and states that causes are hypotheses needing more data; learners present the recommendations per subject. Use a 4-point rubric (model completeness, use of evidence, recognition of limits, clarity of communication).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which groups moved from 'the learners are weak' to 'the decision must be made per subject' and what evidence convinced them? Did learners use the words 'may', 'could' and 'we need more data' when discussing the reasons for the Subject 2 results, or did some assert causes such as a hard test or poor teaching? Which part of the evidence (tables, measures or graphs) did learners use most confidently, and which needs revisiting? Were the grouped estimates (80.5 and 35) clearly distinguished from the exact values (80.35 and 33.85)? How well did the recommendations for the 16 learners below 50 balance support with respect? What would I change about how I used wait time and cold-calling so that quieter learners contributed to the Final Explanation?

Tables, measures and graphs showed these patterns clearly, while the raw lists hid them.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Collecting, organising (ordering, frequency tables) and interpreting (measures and graphs) data shows centre, spread and pass rates, so decisions can be based on evidence. Because the same learners did well in one subject and poorly in the other, decisions must be made per subject. The data cannot tell us why, so causes are hypotheses to be investigated.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Mr. Otieno's class should continue with extension or enrichment work; Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners should reteach and revise the Subject 2 topics and run remedial support for the 16 learners below 50; and more data (topic-by-topic marks, a second test) should be collected to find the cause before concluding. Organised and interpreted data lets us predict and justify next steps for learners and teachers.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Madam Achieng, the Deputy Principal of a day secondary school in Kisumu, has given the Grade 10 class the test scores of the same 20 learners in Subject 1 (Mr. Otieno) and Subject 2 (Mrs. Wanjiku). The pass mark is 50 out of 100. Answer every question in the space under it, using the data from our lessons. Show your working for every calculation. Write grouped-data answers as estimates and give reasons in full sentences. When you talk about WHY the scores differ, say what we cannot yet know and use words such as 'may', 'could' and 'we need more data'. Your answers should help you answer the driving question: How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?

sections.title: Part 1: Organising the scores into frequency tables
sections.prompt:
Here are the scores in ascending order.

Subject 1: 67, 69, 70, 72, 73, 74, 76, 77, 78, 80, 81, 82, 84, 85, 86, 88, 89, 90, 91, 95.

Subject 2: 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 23, 27, 29, 30, 31, 32, 32, 35, 42, 44, 45, 51, 58, 60, 60.

(a) Using a common class width of 10, with classes written 10-19, 20-29, ... up to 90-99, make one grouped frequency table for both subjects. Use tally marks grouped in fives and show the frequency for each subject. Check your totals.
(b) Why did we use the same classes for both subjects?
(c) If you made an ungrouped frequency table for Subject 1, what would you notice, and why does grouping help Madam Achieng more? (Key Inquiry 1: How do we organise data using frequency distribution tables?)
sections.exemplar:
(a) Frequencies (the tally marks match these numbers, written in groups of five):

| Class | Subject 1 f | Subject 2 f |
|---|---|---|
| 10-19 | 0 | 4 |
| 20-29 | 0 | 4 |
| 30-39 | 0 | 5 |
| 40-49 | 0 | 3 |
| 50-59 | 0 | 2 |
| 60-69 | 2 | 2 |
| 70-79 | 7 | 0 |
| 80-89 | 8 | 0 |
| 90-99 | 3 | 0 |
| Total | 20 | 20 |

Both frequency columns add up to n = 20, so every score has been counted once.

(b) Using the same classes lets us compare the two subjects fairly, because each row stands for the same marks in both columns.

(c) In an ungrouped table for Subject 1, every score occurs once (20 different scores, each f = 1). The table would be as long as the list and would show little. Grouping gives 9 short rows that show where the scores cluster: 15 of the 20 Subject 1 scores are in 70-89, while Subject 2 scores are spread from 10-19 to 60-69, with 16 of 20 below 50. A busy teacher can see this pattern at a glance.

sections.title: Part 2: Finding the typical score
sections.prompt:
Use the ordered lists in Part 1 (the sum of the Subject 1 scores is 1607 and the sum of the Subject 2 scores is 677).
(a) Calculate the mean and the median of each subject.
(b) State the mode of each subject, and explain what it means when a set has no mode or two modes.
(c) Compare the typical score in each subject with the pass mark of 50. What does this suggest about whether the learners are weak overall?
sections.exemplar:
(a) Subject 1: mean = 1607 ÷ 20 = 80.35. For the median, n = 20, so we average the 10th and 11th ordered values: (80 + 81) ÷ 2 = 80.5.
Subject 2: mean = 677 ÷ 20 = 33.85. Median = (31 + 32) ÷ 2 = 31.5.

(b) Subject 1 has no mode, because every score occurs only once. Subject 2 has two modes, 32 and 60, because each occurs twice and every other score occurs once; we say it is bimodal. A mode is the most frequent score, so a set can have none, one or more than one.

(c) The typical score in Subject 1 (about 80) is well above the pass mark of 50. The typical score in Subject 2 (about 32 to 34) is below 50. The same 20 learners scored high in one subject and low in the other, so they cannot all be weak. The difference seems to be between the subjects. These measures do not tell us why the scores differ, and they do not show how spread out the scores are.

sections.title: Part 3: Reading position and spread from cumulative frequency
sections.prompt:
The grouped frequencies are:

| Class | Subject 1 f | Subject 2 f |
|---|---|---|
| 10-19 | 0 | 4 |
| 20-29 | 0 | 4 |
| 30-39 | 0 | 5 |
| 40-49 | 0 | 3 |
| 50-59 | 0 | 2 |
| 60-69 | 2 | 2 |
| 70-79 | 7 | 0 |
| 80-89 | 8 | 0 |
| 90-99 | 3 | 0 |

(a) Make a cumulative frequency table for Subject 2 using the upper class boundaries (less-than values).
(b) Using the 5th, 10th and 15th learners, estimate Q1, the median and Q3 for Subject 2, and its interquartile range (IQR). Show your working.
(c) For Subject 1 the estimates are Q1 = 73.8 and Q3 = 87.0. Find its estimated IQR and compare it with that of Subject 2. What does this tell you about the spread of the middle half of the learners in each subject?
(d) Why are these values called estimates?
sections.exemplar:
(a) Subject 2:

| Score less than | 9.5 | 19.5 | 29.5 | 39.5 | 49.5 | 59.5 | 69.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cf | 0 | 4 | 8 | 13 | 16 | 18 | 20 |

(b) Q1 is the 5th learner. It lies in 20-29 (cf before = 4, f = 4): Q1 = 19.5 + (1/4) × 10 = 22.0.
The median is the 10th learner. It lies in 30-39 (cf before = 8, f = 5): median = 29.5 + (2/5) × 10 = 33.5.
Q3 is the 15th learner. It lies in 40-49 (cf before = 13, f = 3): Q3 = 39.5 + (2/3) × 10 = 46.2 (1 dp).
Estimated IQR = 46.2 − 22.0 = 24.2.

(c) Subject 1 estimated IQR = 87.0 − 73.8 = 13.2. Subject 2 has the larger IQR (24.2 compared with 13.2), so the middle half of the Subject 2 scores is more spread out, while the middle half of the Subject 1 scores is close together. This agrees with the ranges: 28 for Subject 1 and 49 for Subject 2.

(d) They are estimates because the grouped table does not show the exact scores. We only know how many scores fall in each class, so we assume the scores are spread evenly within the class. They differ slightly from the exact values from the ungrouped lists, for example 33.5 compared with the exact median of 31.5.

sections.title: Part 4: Claim, evidence and reasoning
sections.prompt:
A classmate says: 'These 20 learners are all weak, so Madam Achieng should tell the whole class to repeat the term.'
(a) Write a claim-evidence-reasoning response. Use at least three pieces of evidence from the tables, measures or graphs (for example pass counts, a measure of centre and a measure of spread).
(b) We saw that Subject 1 histograms and polygons are narrow and to the right, and Subject 2 histograms and polygons are wide and to the left. Explain what this shape tells you that the raw lists did not.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Claim: The learners are not all weak, so the whole class should not repeat the term. The difference is between the subjects.
Evidence: All 20 learners passed Subject 1 (lowest score 67, mean 80.35, median 80.5), but only 4 of 20 passed Subject 2 (16 scored below 50, mean 33.85, median 31.5). The range is 28 in Subject 1 and 49 in Subject 2.
Reasoning: The same 20 learners did very well in one subject. If they were all weak, they would not all pass Subject 1 with scores of 67 or more. So the low Subject 2 results do not describe the learners themselves. Decisions need to be made for each subject separately.

(b) The histograms and polygons show the shape at a glance. Subject 1 is a tight block of bars between 60 and 99, tallest at 80-89 (f = 8). Subject 2 is spread across 10 to 69, tallest at 30-39 (f = 5), and sits much further left. The raw lists were just long rows of numbers. The graphs show the centre, the spread and the position of each subject. They still cannot tell us why the scores differ.

sections.title: Part 5: Recommendations and why data helps decisions
sections.prompt:
Madam Achieng wants a final report that answers the driving question: How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?
(a) Write one evidence-based recommendation each for Mr. Otieno, for Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners, and for the 16 learners who scored below 50 in Subject 2. Link each to the data.
(b) Name two reasons that could explain the difference in scores. Explain why you cannot yet claim that either is the cause, and what further data you would collect.
(c) Answer Key Inquiry 2: Why is it important to collect, organise and interpret data in making decisions? Use what changed between the raw lists and your tables, measures and graphs.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Mr. Otieno: Continue with the Subject 1 teaching and give extension or enrichment work, because all 20 learners passed and the scores are high and close together (mean 80.35, range 28).
Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners: Reteach and revise the Subject 2 topics, because only 4 of 20 passed, the mean is 33.85 and the scores are widely spread (range 49).
The 16 learners below 50 in Subject 2: Run remedial support for them, as they failed at the pass mark of 50. Seven of the 20 scored 40 or more, so some are close to the pass mark.
We predict that these steps could help, but we should also collect more data.

(b) The test in Subject 2 may have been harder, or the teaching method or revision time may have been different. The data we have only shows what the scores were. It does not show the difficulty of the test, the way each subject was taught or the time spent revising, so these are hypotheses to investigate, not facts. We would collect more data, such as topic-by-topic marks and a second test, to find the cause before concluding.

(c) The raw and ordered lists only showed the highest, lowest and pass or fail. They hid the patterns, the spread and what action was needed. When we organised the data into frequency tables and interpreted it with measures and graphs, we could see that Subject 1 is high and tightly clustered while Subject 2 is low and widely spread. This lets us make decisions for each subject, support our recommendations with evidence, and decide what extra data is still needed.

rubric.excellent: Builds a complete, correct grouped table with a common class width of 10, correct tallies and frequencies totalling 20 for each subject, and clearly explains why grouping is more useful than an ungrouped table.
rubric.proficient: Builds a mostly correct table with one small error, and gives a basic reason for using the same classes or for grouping.
rubric.developing: Table has several errors or totals that do not equal 20, or gives no reason for the choice of classes.

rubric.criterion: Calculating measures (mean, median, mode, quartiles, IQR)
rubric.excellent: All measures are correct (80.35, 80.5, 33.85, 31.5, modes 32 and 60, IQR estimates 13.2 and 24.2) with clear working, and grouped values are called estimates with a reason given.
rubric.proficient: Most measures are correct with working shown, with a small slip, or the reason for 'estimate' is incomplete.
rubric.developing: Several measures are incorrect or working is missing, and does not recognise grouped values as estimates.

rubric.excellent: Uses centre, spread, shape and pass rate together to compare the subjects, and explains what the graphs show that the raw lists hid.
rubric.proficient: Uses at least two features (such as the mean and the pass count) to compare the subjects, with limited reference to spread or shape.
rubric.developing: Only lists numbers or describes one subject, with no comparison.

rubric.excellent: Gives a clear claim supported by several correct pieces of evidence, and recommendations for Mr. Otieno, Mrs. Wanjiku, the learners and the 16 learners below 50, each linked to the data.
rubric.proficient: Gives a claim with some evidence and recommendations for most groups, but the link between the data and the recommendation is sometimes weak.
rubric.developing: Claim is unsupported or recommendations are missing or not linked to the data.

rubric.criterion: Separating what the data shows from what it cannot explain
rubric.excellent: Treats reasons for the score difference as hypotheses using words such as 'may' and 'could', and names suitable extra data (topic-by-topic marks, a second test).
rubric.proficient: Recognises that causes are not known but gives an unclear or incomplete plan for finding out.
rubric.developing: States a cause for the score difference as a fact.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can you use the two sets of data to predict the learners' and the teachers' next steps?

lessons.title: The Two Sets of Scores: Phenomenon Launch
lessons.observed: We observed that the same 20 learners scored between 67 and 95 in Subject 1 (range 28, all 20 pass) and between 11 and 60 in Subject 2 (range 49, only 4 pass and 16 fail at a pass mark of 50). Ordering the scores made the highest, lowest and pass/fail easy to see.
lessons.learned: We learned that arranging raw data in ascending order shows the highest, lowest and pass/fail at a glance, but it does not clearly show patterns, spread or the typical score. Reasons for the difference are only hypotheses until we have more data.
lessons.explained: The difference is between the subjects, so we cannot say all 20 learners are weak. To decide next steps for the learners, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku, we need to organise and summarise the data with tables, typical values and graphs, which is what we will do in the coming lessons.

lessons.title: Frequency Distribution Tables for Ungrouped Data: Tallying the Two Sets of Scores
lessons.observed: We tallied the 20 scores in Subject 1 and the 20 scores in Subject 2 into frequency tables with columns Score, Tally and Frequency. In Subject 1 every score occurred once (20 different scores). In Subject 2, 32 and 60 each occurred twice and the other scores once (18 different scores). Both frequency columns added to 20.
lessons.learned: A frequency distribution table for ungrouped data lists each score, a tally (grouped in fives) and the frequency, and the frequencies must add up to n = 20. Tables help us count accurately and spot repeats, but ungrouped tables with many different scores are long and do not yet clearly show where scores cluster or how widely they spread.
lessons.explained: The tables are accurate summaries of how often each score occurs, which helps Madam Achieng, Mr. Otieno and Mrs. Wanjiku check the data. However, Subject 1's table is as long as its list, so we need another way of organising the scores to see patterns and spread. The tables cannot tell us why the subjects differ; that would need more data.

lessons.title: Grouped Frequency Distribution Tables: Choosing Class Intervals and Classifying the Scores
lessons.observed: We organised the 20 scores of Subject 1 and Subject 2 into grouped frequency tables using a common class width of 10 (classes 10-19 to 90-99). Subject 1 frequencies: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 7, 8, 3 and Subject 2 frequencies: 4, 4, 5, 3, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, each totalling 20.
lessons.learned: We learned how to use the range (28 and 49) to choose a class width, write class limits, find class boundaries (9.5, 19.5, ..., 99.5) and midpoints (14.5, ..., 94.5), and classify scores with tally marks so that frequencies add to n = 20.
lessons.explained: Grouping shows that Subject 1 scores cluster high (70-89 has 15 of 20 learners and no score is below 60), while Subject 2 scores are spread out (16 of 20 are below 50). The raw lists hid this pattern. The tables do not tell us why, so we need more data, such as topic-by-topic marks and a second test, before deciding the causes and next steps.

lessons.title: Mean, Mode and Median of Ungrouped Data: Comparing the Two Subjects
lessons.observed: Calculating from the ordered lists and frequency tables, we observed that Subject 1 has a sum of 1607, mean 80.35, median 80.5 and no mode, while Subject 2 has a sum of 677, mean 33.85, median 31.5 and two modes (32 and 60).
lessons.learned: We learned how to calculate the mean (sum of x divided by n), the median (average of the 10th and 11th ordered values when n = 20) and the mode (the most frequent score, which may be none or more than one), and that each gives a different way to describe a typical score.
lessons.explained: The typical score in Subject 1 (about 80) is well above the pass mark of 50, while the typical score in Subject 2 (about 32-34) is below it, so the difference seems to be between subjects and not because the learners are weak overall; the measures may help predict next steps but they do not show spread or the cause, so we need more data.

lessons.title: Mean, Mode and Median of Grouped Data: Estimating the Centre of Each Subject
lessons.observed: We observed that the grouped tables let us estimate the mean (Subject 1: 1610/20 = 80.5; Subject 2: 700/20 = 35), the modal class and mode (80-89, about 81.2; 30-39, about 32.8) and the median (about 80.75 and 33.5). These are close to the exact values from Lesson 4 but not identical.
lessons.learned: We learned how to use midpoints and fx to estimate the mean, boundaries and d1, d2 to estimate the mode, and cumulative frequency to estimate the median. We learned that grouped measures are estimates because each score is replaced by its class midpoint or position in the class.
lessons.explained: We can explain that Subject 1 is centred around 80 and Subject 2 around 34, so decisions must be made per subject: the same learners cannot all be 'weak'. We cannot yet say why the scores differ, and we need spread information and more data before deciding the full next steps.

lessons.title: Representation of Data I: Histograms and Frequency Polygons
lessons.observed: We drew histograms (bars touching at the boundaries 9.5 to 99.5) and frequency polygons (points at midpoints 14.5 to 94.5, closed to the axis) for Subject 1 and Subject 2 on the same axes. Subject 1: scores clustered between 60 and 99, tallest bar 80-89 (f = 8). Subject 2: scores spread from 10 to 69, tallest bar 30-39 (f = 5).
lessons.learned: A histogram shows the frequency of each class with bars at the class boundaries; a frequency polygon joins (midpoint, frequency) points and is closed at the empty classes either side. Using the same classes and scales for both subjects makes the comparison fair, and the graphs make shape and spread easy to see.
lessons.explained: The graphs show that Subject 1 is high and tightly clustered while Subject 2 is low and widely spread, so the difference is between subjects and not about the learners all being weak. The graphs cannot tell us why the scores differ, so we need more data (for example topic-by-topic marks and a second test) before concluding.

lessons.title: Representation of Data II: Cumulative Frequency and Ogives
lessons.observed: We observed that the cumulative frequency of Subject 2 reaches 13 by 39.5 and 20 by 69.5, while Subject 1 stays at 0 until 59.5 and then rises to 20 by 99.5. Both ogives were drawn using (upper boundary, cf) points. From the ogives we read estimates: Subject 1 Q1 73.8, median 80.75, Q3 87.0; Subject 2 Q1 22.0, median 33.5, Q3 46.2.
lessons.learned: We learned that a cumulative frequency table adds up the frequencies to show how many learners scored below each upper boundary, and that an ogive lets us read the median (10th), Q1 (5th) and Q3 (15th) as estimates. The IQR = Q3 - Q1 is 13.2 for Subject 1 and 24.2 for Subject 2, so the middle half of Subject 2 scores is more spread out.
lessons.explained: The ogives help us to answer the driving question by showing position and spread: Subject 1 scores are high and close together, while Subject 2 scores are lower and more spread out, with a median estimate of 33.5. This supports predictions that Mr. Otieno's class may continue with extension work and that Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners may reteach and revise, give support to the learners below 50 and collect more data. The graphs show what happened but not why, so we need more data such as topic-by-topic marks and a second test before concluding.

lessons.title: Interpretation of Data: Comparing Subjects and Predicting Next Steps
lessons.observed: We observed that Subject 1 scores are high and tightly clustered (mean 80.35, median 80.5, range 28, all 20 learners pass) while Subject 2 scores are low and widely spread (mean 33.85, median 31.5, range 49, only 4 of 20 pass, 16 below 50, 7 at 40 or more). The histograms, polygons and ogives show the same pattern: the Subject 1 graphs are narrow and to the right, and the Subject 2 graphs are wide and to the left.
lessons.learned: We learned that tables, measures and graphs must be read together to compare two sets of data using average, spread, shape and pass rate. We learned that the grouped values are estimates, and that the data shows differences between subjects but cannot tell us why the scores differ.
lessons.explained: We explain that the same 20 learners cannot all be weak, because they all passed Subject 1 but most failed Subject 2, so decisions must be made per subject. We predict that Mr. Otieno's class should continue with extension or enrichment work, and that Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners should reteach and revise the Subject 2 topics, give remedial support to the 16 learners below 50, and collect more data (such as topic-by-topic marks and a second test) before concluding why the scores differ.

lessons.title: Why Collecting, Organising and Interpreting Data Leads to Effective Decisions
lessons.observed: Same 20 learners: Subject 1 scores 67 to 95 (mean 80.35, median 80.5, range 28, all 20 pass); Subject 2 scores 11 to 60 (mean 33.85, median 31.5, range 49, only 4 pass, 16 below 50, 7 at 40 or above). Tables, measures and graphs showed these patterns clearly, while the raw lists hid them.
lessons.learned: Collecting, organising (ordering, frequency tables) and interpreting (measures and graphs) data shows centre, spread and pass rates, so decisions can be based on evidence. Because the same learners did well in one subject and poorly in the other, decisions must be made per subject. The data cannot tell us why, so causes are hypotheses to be investigated.
lessons.explained: Mr. Otieno's class should continue with extension or enrichment work; Mrs. Wanjiku and the learners should reteach and revise the Subject 2 topics and run remedial support for the 16 learners below 50; and more data (topic-by-topic marks, a second test) should be collected to find the cause before concluding. Organised and interpreted data lets us predict and justify next steps for learners and teachers.
